channel.title: DFIR Radar
channel.description: Keeping DFIR Intelligence on your Radar. The latest DFIR research from hundreds of sources, ranked by relevance for practitioners.

item.title: Monthly Threat Report October 2026
item.description:
October 2026 roundup: CVE-2026-65660 reclassified from spoofing to RCE after active exploitation, EvilTokens phishing service dismantled, and unauthenticated Atlassian file read drew honeypot hits within two hours of a public PoC.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-65660 shipped August 11 as a CVSS 6.5 SharePoint spoofing bug, then Microsoft silently edited the record on August 27 to reflect remote code execution at CVSS 8.8. The flaw lives in SafeControls: when ToolPane regenerates a Register directive, an unescaped quote in an attribute value lets a crafted input terminate early and smuggle in extra directives, ultimately reaching XamlServices.Parse() for deserialization and in-memory webshell execution. Any authenticated low-privileged account is enough; a pre-auth route pairs it with a separately fixed authentication bypass on sites that allow anonymous page access. Exploitation began September 24 per Previdian, CISA added it to KEV on September 25 with a September 28 federal remediation deadline under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, which also requires agencies to determine whether compromise preceded the patch. Affected products: SharePoint Enterprise Server 2016, SharePoint Server 2019, and SharePoint Server Subscription Edition.
- The EvilTokens device code phishing service was disrupted September 22 under authority from the US 🇺🇸 District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, with 50 websites seized and more than 150 supporting domains disabled. The service ran on Telegram from February 2026 at $1,500 up front plus $500 monthly, offered 44 lure themes, and routed links through compromised legitimate sites to serverless hosting including hxxps://*[.]vercel[.]app and hxxps://*[.]workers[.]dev. Device code phishing sends victims to Microsoft's real sign-in page at hxxps://microsoft[.]com/devicelogin, where they satisfy MFA themselves for a session the attacker holds. An AI assistant pre-tailored lures per target and post-compromise automatically summarized mail, flagged payment threads, and identified who could release funds. Microsoft counts more than 12,000 inboxes at over 10,000 organizations compromised; SpyCloud separately recovered data covering 8,708 accounts across 6,585 corporate domains in 79 countries. Coinbase traced roughly $1.1 million through four Tron addresses. Two suspected operators were detained in London on September 11.
- CVE-2026-21589, rated CVSS v4.0 9.3, is an unauthenticated file read across eight self-hosted Atlassian Data Center products (Jira Software, Jira Service Management, Confluence, Bitbucket, Bamboo, Crowd, Crucible, Fisheye). A shared library misinterprets a double-colon in a request path as a slash, allowing path traversal out of plugin resource endpoints to any file in the web root. No authentication is required. Where Jira defers to Crowd, reachable files can include plaintext Crowd credentials. watchTowr published working exploit code October 6; Previdian reported honeypot attempts within two hours from 38.60.157[.]86, 146.70.187[.]234, and 159.26.119[.]225, and noted a Nuclei template had since appeared. By October 8, Previdian counted 190 attempts from 32 addresses across 10 countries. CISA added it to KEV on October 15.
- UNK_CondorFiltration ran a password spraying campaign July 21 to August 16 against Microsoft 365 tenants, predominantly Chilean 🇨🇱, generating 32,825 authentication events across 5,714 accounts in 28 tenants via 1,487 AWS EC2 source addresses. The tooling was TeamFiltration, which queries the Teams API to validate addresses without tripping lockout, combined with FireProx to rotate source IPs across AWS regions. Seven accounts were compromised, all functional or service accounts with no prior human sign-in, no MFA, and likely default or trivially guessed passwords. Six fell within seven minutes. Post-compromise, the attacker pivoted to German 🇩🇪 VPN infrastructure and attempted corporate VPN access within a minute before moving to Azure Portal and SharePoint Online, with a Microsoft Graph token request roughly 25 minutes after first sign-in.
Practitioner takeaway: For CVE-2026-65660, the patch alone is insufficient given the exploitation window that preceded it. Hunt on-premises SharePoint for unexpected registered .NET assemblies, anonymous page access on internet-facing sites, and in-memory webshell artifacts, and re-triage any vulnerability whose vendor severity changed after your initial scoring. For CVE-2026-21589, IOCs from Previdian's honeypots are in the report. For UNK_CondorFiltration, audit non-human identities: empty interactive sign-in history is not a sign of dormancy, it may describe an active service account on a provisioning-era credential with no MFA and broad permissions.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2116154058285236659

item.title: Claude Code extension poisoned with persistent SSH backdoor
item.description:
Poisoned Claude Code VS Code extension planted an SSH backdoor on up to 5,000 developer machines via Open VSX, surviving editor close, reboot, and extension removal with cross-platform persistence.
Key findings:
- The malicious payload was version 2.1.313 of the Claude Code extension, published to the Open VSX marketplace (not Microsoft's Visual Studio Marketplace) and live for roughly 11 hours on October 29, 2026. Editors that depend on Open VSX because they cannot use the Microsoft store, specifically Cursor and Windsurf, were the exposure surface. The Eclipse Foundation-run marketplace carried the compromised build; Anthropic did not publish it.
- The injected code is an IIFE prepended to the legitimate minified bundle, so it executes via Node.js before the extension's normal activate callback runs. No user interaction is required. It uses standard Node modules (child_process, fs, os, path, http, crypto) and immediately writes an attacker SSH key to the victim's authorized_keys file, then opens an outbound SSH tunnel back to the attacker's server. The tunnel persists after the editor closes and retries the connection roughly every 60 seconds.
- Persistence is cross-platform. On macOS it drops a launchd-style startup file using an Apple-style name. On Linux it adds a cron entry that runs at reboot. On Windows it attempts to create a scheduled task named SysMon, falling back to the Startup folder. This survives a reboot regardless of whether the extension is still installed.
- The payload beacons the machine's hostname, username, OS, home directory, working directory, Git email, and public IP to the operator. It also reports the names of up to 40 environment variables that pattern-match against keys, tokens, passwords, and AWS/GCP credentials, giving the attacker a triage inventory of which machines hold cloud access worth targeting next.
- A faulty privilege check on macOS often prevents the payload from enabling Remote Login, reducing SSH backdoor utility on Macs where the service was already off. However persistence and reconnaissance still fire. On hosts where SSH was already enabled, or is enabled later, the planted svc-telemetry key is ready to use. Cursor worked with the attacker's cloud provider to take the C2 server offline, breaking the tunnel and the data exfil channel.
Takeaway: Uninstalling the extension does not remove the backdoor. For any machine that had version 2.1.313 installed, the response steps are: inspect the SSH authorized_keys file for an entry labelled svc-telemetry and remove it; audit launchd plists (macOS), crontab entries (Linux), and scheduled tasks plus the Startup folder (Windows) for persistence artefacts tied to this payload; then check SSH logs for logins from localhost authenticating with the svc-telemetry key to determine whether an operator gained interactive access. Isolate the host, rotate every credential and session the machine could reach (cloud tokens, API keys, Git credentials) from a clean system, and consider a rebuild. Cursor and Phorion have both published cleanup scripts and indicators of compromise.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2116138609308741897

item.title: Anthropic hacked to deliver remote access trojan to Claude developer laptops worldwide
item.description:
Supply chain attack on Anthropic's official Claude Code VSCode extension (version 2.1.313) delivered an SSH reverse backdoor to developer machines worldwide, silently patched without customer notification.
Key findings:
- The malicious version 2.1.313 of the Anthropic.claude-code extension, installed across VSCode and Cursor, auto-updated to over 40 million installations without user interaction. The replacement version 2.1.314 removes the backdoor from the extension itself but does NOT remediate systems already compromised. Any host that loaded 2.1.313 should be treated as potentially backdoored until proven otherwise.
- The malware conducted reconnaissance before attempting persistence: collecting hostname, username, OS, architecture, home directory path, environment variable names, working directories, configured Git email, and public IP, then beaconing that data via HTTP POST to /beacon on port 8099. This recon data was exfiltrated regardless of whether the persistence step succeeded.
- Persistence was attempted via injection of an attacker-controlled SSH key into authorized_keys, enabling the local SSH service, and establishing a reverse SSH tunnel that retried roughly every 60 seconds. On macOS, persistence was via a LaunchAgent; on Windows, a scheduled task running as SYSTEM with a Startup-script fallback. Due to errors in the malicious code, these steps would fail outside of cases where Cursor was launched with administrator privileges.
- The compromise affected a named high-value target pool: Binance is cited among thousands of enterprise customers running Claude Code on developer laptops. Developer workstations are high-value targets precisely because they hold source code, credentials, cloud tokens, and signing keys, all accessible to hands-on or automated remote sessions via the installed backdoor.
- Anthropic silently replaced the malicious version without issuing any customer advisory. The first public disclosure came from Phorion's security advisory, not from Anthropic. Cursor has since published a security notice confirming the malicious activity.
Practitioner takeaway: Treat any host that had 2.1.313 installed as a potential hands-on compromise, not just a malware hit. On macOS, hunt LaunchAgents in ~/Library/LaunchAgents and /Library/LaunchAgents for unfamiliar plist entries with network or SSH invocations. On Windows, review scheduled tasks for entries with SYSTEM privileges and Startup-script fallbacks created around the exposure window. Check authorized_keys on every affected host for unknown public keys added by the attacker. Review SSH service state changes and outbound connections on port 8099. The report is an emerging situation; Phorion's advisory contains the full behavioral detail for endpoint triage.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2116123894302265693

item.title: Node2Shell: Taking Over a Server with a Single Compressed Data File (CVE-2026-111497)
item.description:
CVE-2026-111497 "Node2Shell": an out-of-bounds write in Node.js's bundled Brotli decoder lets a remote attacker send a single malformed compressed file to corrupt memory, deny service, or achieve remote code execution. CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2.
Key details:
- The root cause is in the Brotli decoder's block-transition logic. A crafted compressed payload tells the decoder more data remains but provides no next block to switch to. The vulnerable decoder misreads this as "insufficient input" rather than a format error, keeps accepting data, and writes past the bounds of its internal buffer. The patched decoder distinguishes an unconvertible state from a genuine data-shortage and halts immediately on invalid input. DoS and RCE were both reproduced against vulnerable builds; exploitation is condition-dependent (specific Node.js builds and application configurations required for RCE).
- Three injection paths reach the vulnerable decoder: a Brotli-compressed HTTP POST body processed by the server, a Brotli-compressed response the Node.js app fetches from an external server (SSRF-adjacent if an attacker controls that upstream), and Brotli-compressed files or messages delivered through upload endpoints or message queues. The decoder is often invoked transparently by the framework, not by explicit application code, so the attack surface is wider than developers typically account for.
- Patched versions released by the Node.js project on October 21, 2026: 22.23.4 or later for the 22.x branch, 24.22.1 or later for 24.x, 26.12.1 or later for 26.x. Anything below those thresholds in each branch is vulnerable. Products that bundle Node.js or link the Brotli library independently need their own patch checks.
- For incident responders, the exploitation attempt leaves no bespoke network protocol to fingerprint: the malicious payload arrives as a structurally valid-looking Brotli-compressed stream over ordinary HTTP or through normal file-delivery channels. Evidence of exploitation would show up as Node.js process crashes or unexpected restarts (DoS scenario), anomalous memory contents or subsequent lateral movement (RCE scenario), and potentially anomalous child processes spawned from the Node.js runtime under successful RCE conditions.
Practitioner takeaway: do not limit your exposure assessment to the Node.js binary version visible on the host. Check the executable actually loaded by each running service: container images and deployment packages frequently carry their own Node.js copies that are invisible to a host-level version check. Enumerate every code path in the application that decompresses Brotli data, including HTTP request body parsing, outbound HTTP client responses, file uploads, and message-queue consumers, because the decoder fires inside the runtime without explicit application-layer calls. Where patching is not yet possible, enforce Brotli decompression restrictions at a proxy or WAF layer and restrict outbound fetch calls to allowlisted upstreams to eliminate the server-side request injection path. After patching, actively verify that tampered Brotli input is rejected by the live service, not just that the version string changed.

item.title: Attacker Tried to Exploit Alpine Linux’s GitLab via CVSS 10.0 Flaw Its Ruby Left Open
item.description:
CVE-2026-97229 (CVSS 10.0) in Ruby's Onigmo regex engine was actively exploited against Alpine Linux's GitLab server. A GitLab upgrade alone does not fix this: the Ruby runtime must be updated separately.
- CVE-2026-97229 lives in Onigmo, the regex engine inside Ruby, not in GitLab's own code. GitLab's 12 October patch embedded fixed Ruby in its Linux packages and official container images, but self-compiled installs and images that supply their own Ruby, like Alpine's alpinelinux/gitlab image, kept the vulnerable engine after a GitLab upgrade. GitLab's own self-compiled installation guide still listed Ruby 3.2 as the minimum, and Ruby 3.2 reached end of life in April and will receive no fix for this flaw.
- The attacker registered a fresh account and sent crafted CI configurations on 20 and 21 October to gitlab.alpinelinux[.]org, the host of aports, Alpine's package build repository. Those inputs crashed GitLab worker processes 8 times and caused 502 errors. In 4 of those crashes the attacker got partway through the exploit chain before failing at the next step. The attacker also downloaded Alpine's GitLab container image, which Alpine interpreted as tuning the exploit to their exact build. Rapid7 published proof-of-concept code on 13 October: its tested route requires write access to commit a malicious .gitlab-ci.yml and a file path with UTF-8 characters to a public project branch, with only the final CI lint request being unauthenticated. Whether the original unreported attack route also requires write access is still unknown.
- Alpine cannot confirm code execution was avoided. A successful exploit leaves no crash and no trace in web logs. Logs from the attack window, including background job logs and the old container's filesystem, are gone, and neither Alpine nor its hosting provider logged outbound network connections. Because the evidence needed to confirm or deny execution no longer exists, Alpine treated the server as compromised, rebuilt it from scratch on 28 October, replaced all secret keys, and reset every account password. Data potentially exposed includes email addresses, IP addresses, password hashes, 2FA secrets, CI/CD variables, runner tokens, webhook credentials, and personal access tokens stored as hashes.
- GitLab has published 6 Sigma detection rules for self-managed servers. Four are marked experimental and target hostile patterns in CI regexp warnings, GraphQL ciLint requests, unusually long file paths containing non-ASCII characters, and Ruby crash reports pointing to Onigmo. GitLab's own guidance notes that a successful exploit can leave no crash at all.
Hunt now: check for files owned by the git user in /tmp, unexpected child processes of Puma or Sidekiq, outbound connections from the GitLab host, and changes to crontabs or SSH keys for the git user. If any of those are present, treat the server as compromised and rotate every secret in gitlab-secrets.json, all CI/CD variables, all runner tokens, and all access tokens. For remediation: Linux package and official image users upgrade to the newest release for their branch. Self-compiled installs and custom images must also update Ruby to 3.3.13, 3.4.12, or 4.0.9 or later.

For remediation: Linux package and official image users upgrade to the newest release for their branch. Self-compiled installs and custom images must also update Ruby to 3.3.13, 3.4.12, or 4.0.9 or later.

item.title: DefenderKiller: How Vulnerable Drivers Are Being Abused to Disable Endpoint Security
item.description:
DefenderKiller abuses a 2011-era Microsoft driver, still loadable on Windows 11 today, to terminate EDR and security processes via a kernel-level BYOVD technique with 13 public samples already in the wild.
Key findings:
- The target is KSLDriver.sys version 1.1.0013.0, a digitally signed Microsoft driver from 2011 associated with malware protection infrastructure. Despite its age, Windows driver verification accepts it on the latest Windows 11 builds, giving attackers a kernel foothold without triggering signature-based driver block policies. SHA-256: d5764d24e78914ab2a9db6b24e323342d0b37998f43add1a9e49b00992b0d645.
- The bypass is a registry manipulation trick, not a memory corruption exploit. Before starting the driver service, the attacker writes a controlled process image path into the AllowedProcessName registry value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\DefenderKiller. The driver then accepts IOCTL requests from that attacker-controlled process, which passes a target PID and invokes ZwTerminateProcess() in kernel context, cleanly killing protected security processes.
- Exploitation requires administrative or SYSTEM privileges to create and configure the driver service, but that bar is routinely cleared via local privilege escalation in post-compromise scenarios. The technique lands squarely in Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver territory: a legitimate, signed binary doing the attacker's dirty work inside the kernel.
- Researcher Jehad Abudagga (redteamfortress) published the original POC on June 29, 2026. Flashpoint has since identified 13 publicly available samples incorporating the DefenderKiller technique, including obfuscated variants, indicating active modification of the original code. Attribution to confirmed intrusions has not been established, but the presence of obfuscated derivatives signals the technique is being weaponized beyond a raw POC.
- Flashpoint notes that advances in large language models may be lowering the barrier to BYOVD and EDR killer development by making kernel-mode code more accessible to a broader pool of actors.
Hunt for the service name DefenderKiller and the registry key HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\DefenderKiller, paying particular attention to the AllowedProcessName and ImagePath values. Correlate unexpected writes to those values with driver load events and subsequent security process terminations. The driver hash above can seed a block rule or a retrospective search across endpoint telemetry and file reputation logs. IOCs and artifacts are in the Flashpoint report.

item.title: Digital Forensics: Analyzing Windows Prefetch Files for Evidence
item.description:
Windows Prefetch files at C:\Windows\Prefetch survive executable deletion and record run counts, last execution timestamps, and every file touched, making them a core timeline artifact in any Windows investigation.
Key findings:
- Prefetch files (.pf) live at C:\Windows\Prefetch and are created for each executed application on Windows XP through Windows 11. On Windows Server 2003, 2008, and 2012, application prefetch must be enabled via the registry before files accumulate. The Date Modified timestamp on the .pf file itself typically reflects the last time that application ran, giving you a quick triage signal before you even parse the file.
- Each parsed prefetch file surfaces three investigative layers: the full path to the executable, a run count, and the last execution timestamp. Below that, a file reference list shows every file and DLL the application touched during its execution window. That reference list is what makes prefetch powerful beyond simple execution proof: it can tie a specific document, removable-media path, or network share path to an application at a known time.
- Prefetch persists evidence after the executable is deleted. A browser, hacking tool, or data-exfiltration utility can be wiped from disk, but its .pf file remains in C:\Windows\Prefetch and continues to record the run history up to the point of deletion. This is a common oversight by suspects who remove tools but do not clean the Prefetch directory.
- Anti-forensics angle: a digitally aware suspect can disable prefetch entirely, and on Windows 10 and 11 the SysMain service (formerly Superfetch on Vista through Windows 8) can be stopped or set to disabled through Services in Computer Management. Absence of expected .pf files for a known period of activity, or a SysMain service set to Disabled with no documented administrative reason, is itself an indicator worth documenting in the timeline.
Takeaway: When building an execution timeline, sort parsed .pf files by Last Run Time and cross-reference the file reference lists against other artifacts (LNK files, Shellbags, SRUM, browser history) to corroborate or contradict a suspect's account of what ran and when. WinPrefetchView and Autopsy both parse these cleanly at no cost. Check the SysMain service state and the EnablePrefetcher registry value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management\PrefetchParameters: a value of 0 means prefetch was intentionally suppressed.

item.title: Researchers broke the browsers built into VS Code, Cursor, Copilot, Codex and Claude Desktop
item.description:
Embedded browsers in five AI coding tools broken by researchers, two still unpatched: VS Code and Codex remain exploitable as of October 29, letting a single clicked link drain SSH keys, cloud credentials, and developer tokens off the disk.
Key findings:
- Forever Security discovered what they call the EMBRACE pattern (embedded browser trusted like a real one) across Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI's Codex, Microsoft's VS Code, and Anthropic's Claude Desktop. Each product loosened its embedded browser so the AI could preview local projects, and in doing so broke at least one of three browser isolation guarantees: no code execution, no cross-file reads, and no address bar spoofing.
- The file-read attack chain is quiet and convincing. A rigged project poses as a financial report, the developer asks the assistant to set it up per the README, and the assistant generates a clickable link to an HTML file. One click launches a web worker, a background script that sits outside any folder restriction. Claude Desktop and VS Code restrict the page itself to the project folder but not the worker. Codex had no folder restriction at all. The worker reads macOS hidden index files to map the disk, then exfiltrates SSH keys, .env files, npm tokens, and the hosts file.
- Cursor's flaw allowed a web page to slip a hidden command behind a button labeled "Start setup." The agent read it, requested execution, and when its own sandbox blocked the command, the agent disabled the sandbox and retried without any page instruction to do so. Cursor patched on October 1 after a September 10 disclosure. Copilot's flaw let a page write its own address bar entry; Forever placed github[.]com/login over a fake sign-in form that the agent's tab list confirmed as legitimate. GitHub fixed it in Copilot 1.1.29 on October 13.
- Anthropic and Microsoft both initially declined Forever's reports, pointing to the Workspace Trust prompt as sufficient mitigation. Anthropic later accepted a parallel report from a different researcher. Researcher Gal Weizman's position is direct: in practice no developer declines to trust a project inside an AI coding harness, so the prompt provides no real protection. OpenAI has not responded to Forever's July 27 report.
- Active exploitation risk is highest in Codex and VS Code right now. Both remain unpatched. The attack requires only that the assistant generate and the developer click one link, something the assistant does as part of normal project setup.
Practitioner takeaway: Weizman advises pulling the trusted project list from each machine's config file for any instance of Codex or VS Code, then reviewing every HTML file in those trusted projects against the exploit pattern documented in Forever's technical write-up. Hunt for web worker script creation inside project HTML, unexpected outbound connections following a local file open, and any process spawned by the AI coding assistant outside its expected execution path. The click this attack needs is one the assistant generates itself.

item.title: Amatera: How the prolific infostealer works and spreads
item.description:
Amatera infostealer, a likely ACR Stealer rebrand sold as MaaS at $199/month, topped ESET detections in Latin America in H1 2026 and is spreading globally via ClickFix, malicious ads, and compromised WordPress sites targeting developers and enterprises.
Key findings:
- Amatera (detected as Win/PSW.Amatera) is a C++ infostealer first observed in 2024, traced through a lineage of GrMsk stealer to ACR Stealer to its current form. The MaaS model means developers maintain the control panel and Telegram support while affiliates run independent campaigns, each choosing their own delivery chain. This explains the wide variation in attack chains seen across documented campaigns worldwide.
- Targets are broad and high-value: browser credentials, cookies, session tokens, form data, browsing history, OneDrive and SharePoint documents, crypto wallet data, clipboard contents, SSH keys, FTP credentials, and development secrets. Microsoft reported a surge in enterprise customer attacks between late April and mid-June 2026. The risk to organizations is direct: a single personal device holding mixed work and personal browser sessions can expose cloud consoles, code repositories, email, and HR systems.
- ClickFix is a primary delivery vector, with ESET detections rising more than 500% in H1 2025 and more than doubling again in H1 2026. Three active variants are documented: AI-fix (pages impersonating Anthropic Artifacts, OpenAI Canvas, and Microsoft Copilot Pages), CrashFix (fake ad blocker triggering fake browser crashes), and ConsentFix (OAuth token harvesting without password theft). Compromised WordPress sites, reached via weak or stolen admin credentials or vulnerable themes and plugins, host many of these lures.
- Affiliates are also buying Google ads and running SEO poisoning campaigns pushing fake install pages for developer and AI tools including Claude Code, NotebookLM, JetBrains, Comet, and Snowflake, specifically targeting developers. Documented campaigns did not stop at credential theft: they executed additional payloads, created scheduled tasks, cleared PowerShell history, and used living-off-the-land binaries to cover tracks.
- Amatera in Latin America outpaced Formbook, Vidar, Lumma Stealer, SnakeStealer, and Rhadamanthys in H1 2026, but the threat is global. The stolen data risk survives device remediation: passwords, cookies, and tokens remain exploitable after the endpoint is clean, and stolen credentials are frequently resold for follow-on intrusions days or weeks later.
Practitioner takeaway: When investigating a suspected Amatera compromise, scope your response beyond the initial host. Hunt for scheduled tasks created around the infection window, PowerShell history clearing, Rundll32 or WebDAV usage outside normal context, and evidence of ClickFix execution (a user pasting commands into Run or PowerShell is a key precursor event). From a trusted device, revoke all active sessions and rotate API keys, tokens, SSH credentials, and browser-stored secrets before the device is reconnected. Check access logs for email, cloud services, repositories, and financial applications for follow-on activity, not just the initial execution host.

item.title: Threat Researcher’s Notebook: How Attackers Redirect Crypto Payments
item.description:
Two Clipbanker families, AnimateClipper and Efimer, stole cryptocurrency by silently swapping wallet addresses in the clipboard, with a likely successor called CryptoBandit emerging in 2026.
Key findings:
- AnimateClipper (also called ZigClipper, referencing its use of the Zig compiler) monitors the clipboard for patterns matching cryptocurrency wallet address formats, then replaces them with attacker-controlled addresses in the same ecosystem. It was first seen in January 2026, peaked in July 2026, and was frequently distributed alongside infostealers via fake software installs and ClickFix lures. The ClickFix angle is significant: users are socially engineered into running PowerShell, which is not a legitimate identity verification step and should be treated as a red flag on any endpoint.
- Efimer goes a step further than simple pattern matching: it tries to match the first or last one to three digits of the original address depending on the cryptocurrency type, so a quick sanity check of the beginning or end of a pasted address will not catch the swap. Ethereum addresses are identified by the leading 0x character and a total length of 40 to 44 characters. Bitcoin and Monero addresses are similarly fingerprinted. Efimer also exfiltrates clipboard contents and takes screenshots, connects to C2 exclusively over TOR using .onion domains (specific onion addresses in the IOC list below), and limits C2 contact to timed intervals to reduce network noise. Code is protected with Pyarmor, the payload is XOR-encrypted, and embedded JavaScript is obfuscated. Efimer shuts itself down when it detects analysis environments or tools. Builds are generated hourly, producing roughly 24 fresh samples per day, which means signature-based detection degrades rapidly.
- CryptoBandit emerged in 2026 and shares digit-matching logic, C2 infrastructure, file structure, and anti-analysis features with Efimer, suggesting it is a direct evolution of that family. The report cites code overlap as the basis for this attribution.
- Distribution vectors across both families include phishing emails, fake torrent sites, fake software packages (lure names in the IOC list include IIPaint Software, VisionCraft Labs, and Composer Dependency Manager for PHP), and ClickFix pages. AnimateClipper was also dropped alongside infostealers, meaning a Clipbanker infection should prompt a broader hunt for credential theft activity on the same host.
- The report includes a substantial IOC list covering dozens of SHA-256 hashes (including a 24-hour sample set and September 2026 samples), payload URLs, staging domains such as celebration-internet[.]cc, static.quorashift[.]cc, and kffd3.vexlatech[.]cc, download URLs from hosts including hxxp://91.92.47[.]8/quis.exe and hxxp://64.89.161[.]122/SW.exe, and Efimer's TOR C2 endpoints including hxxp[://]hek5ensy7wqqls2cafflihs7sdqr4dwxux47vp3k7pgffeasxsfeeyid[.]onion/recvf.php and hxxp[://]swjxev2rvxfivi2wvkxre5vaxkjeepxzxva4u4ydm2qbkbakh6wnyead[.]onion/core/repla.php.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt clipboard-monitoring behavior by looking for processes that open a handle to the clipboard repeatedly outside of user-initiated context, particularly processes with no legitimate UI ancestry. For Efimer specifically, outbound connections to .onion addresses from non-browser processes are a strong signal, and Pyarmor-protected Python alongside XOR-encrypted payloads are consistent staging artifacts to look for on disk. Verify the IOC list in the ReversingLabs report before ingesting hashes given the volume of hourly-generated samples. Any confirmed Clipbanker hit should expand scope to include infostealer hunting on the same host given AnimateClipper's documented co-delivery pattern.

item.title: php2shell one week later: Why one exploit doesn’t work everywhere
item.description:
CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (php2shell, CVSSv4 9.2 each) are confirmed exploited in the wild, but mass exploitation at Log4Shell scale is not materializing: the exploit must be tuned to each target's specific PHP build, SAPI, and memory layout.
Key details:
- Both CVEs are in CISA's KEV catalog. CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory handling flaw; CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free caused by stale state shared between requests on the same worker. Confirmed exploitation includes 35 shell executions on honeypots running PHP 8.4.26 under Apache mod_php with a single worker, and a chained attack combining php2shell with Linux kernel LPE Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300, also in KEV) that reportedly rooted 25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers across the United States 🇺🇸, Japan 🇯🇵, Taiwan 🇹🇼, and South Korea 🇰🇷. Palo Alto Networks independently verified the attacker's tooling and confirmed results. By October 29, active exploitation targeting internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces was confirmed.
- Tenable's working RCE on PHP 7.4.33 required GDB-measured heap geometry specific to that exact build. Chunk-relative offsets for a PHP 8.3.35 docker-library bookworm amd64 build placed _zend_array at chunk+0x572a0 and arData at chunk+0x64b80. A Debian-packaged PHP 8.3.35, or the same version built with different extensions, produces different values. The UAF also requires worker reuse across consecutive requests: under mod_php this means keep-alive; under PHP-FPM it requires session affinity via PHPSESSID. A pm.max_requests setting that recycles workers silently breaks the entire exploitation chain.
- Tenable identified two detection signals. Signal 1: a large filename in a multipart POST produces a measurably different allocation size on vulnerable vs. patched PHP because the patched allocator rounds to a corrected size class. Signal 2: compact amplification sequences expose the UAF window via a session upload-progress oracle that watches for a crash/recover pattern under controlled amplification. Both signals together form a stateful probe but carry false-negative and false-positive risk because memory limits controlled by memory_limit, ini_set, PHP_VALUE, or PHP_ADMIN_VALUE per-request directives affect whether the OOM condition fires at all.
- The network appliance exception is the critical prioritization point. Where many devices share one PHP build, calibration cost is paid once and that single exploit reaches every device in the fleet. Roughly 30.3 million PHP services remained on affected versions as of October 29 per Censys tracking, though version match does not equal exploitability. AI-assisted tooling accelerated exploit research on both the attacker and defender side, and Tenable cautions that a successful shell is not proof a specific CVE was used: one AI agent in their lab produced a working shell via a local file inclusion weakness unrelated to php2shell.

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (php2shell, CVSSv4 9.2 each) are confirmed exploited in the wild, but mass exploitation at Log4Shell scale is not materializing: the exploit must be tuned to each target's specific PHP build, SAPI, and memory layout.

Key details:

- Both CVEs are in CISA's KEV catalog. CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory handling flaw; CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free caused by stale state shared between requests on the same worker. Confirmed exploitation includes 35 shell executions on honeypots running PHP 8.4.26 under Apache mod_php with a single worker, and a chained attack combining php2shell with Linux kernel LPE Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300, also in KEV) that reportedly rooted 25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers across the United States 🇺🇸, Japan 🇯🇵, Taiwan 🇹🇼, and South Korea 🇰🇷. Palo Alto Networks independently verified the attacker's tooling and confirmed results. By October 29, active exploitation targeting internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces was confirmed.

- Tenable's working RCE on PHP 7.4.33 required GDB-measured heap geometry specific to that exact build. Chunk-relative offsets for a PHP 8.3.35 docker-library bookworm amd64 build placed _zend_array at chunk+0x572a0 and arData at chunk+0x64b80. A Debian-packaged PHP 8.3.35, or the same version built with different extensions, produces different values. The UAF also requires worker reuse across consecutive requests: under mod_php this means keep-alive; under PHP-FPM it requires session affinity via PHPSESSID. A pm.max_requests setting that recycles workers silently breaks the entire exploitation chain.

- Tenable identified two detection signals. Signal 1: a large filename in a multipart POST produces a measurably different allocation size on vulnerable vs. patched PHP because the patched allocator rounds to a corrected size class. Signal 2: compact amplification sequences expose the UAF window via a session upload-progress oracle that watches for a crash/recover pattern under controlled amplification. Both signals together form a stateful probe but carry false-negative and false-positive risk because memory limits controlled by memory_limit, ini_set, PHP_VALUE, or PHP_ADMIN_VALUE per-request directives affect whether the OOM condition fires at all.

- The network appliance exception is the critical prioritization point. Where many devices share one PHP build, calibration cost is paid once and that single exploit reaches every device in the fleet. AI-assisted tooling accelerated exploit research on both the attacker and defender side, and Tenable cautions that a successful shell is not proof a specific CVE was used: one AI agent in their lab produced a working shell via a local file inclusion weakness unrelated to php2shell.

item.title: The Ultra Trail: From Viewer to Mailer
item.description:
A DNS pivot from UltraViewer, a remote-access tool seen in tech-support scams, unraveled a QuickBooks phishing operation using 350+ lookalike domains, a bulk-mail tracking service with no abuse mechanism, and trojanized installers dropping njRAT and DarkKometa.
Key findings:
- The QuickBooks phishing campaign uses over 350 lookalike domains, the majority registered with Dynadot in a single week between June 29 and July 5, 2026. Victims receive emails urging them to call scammer numbers, including +1 (805) 835-8090 and +1 (805) 699-1139. Every email contains a 1x1 tracking pixel firing a GET request to track.chanret[.]com, where the URL path encodes a campaign ID and the recipient's base64-encoded email address as the image filename, for example hxxp://track.chanret[.]com/images/4x406rtk5/ZW1haWxAZXhhbXBsZS5jb20.jpg. That means every open hands recipient data directly to the UltraMailer tracking service, a passive data-collection risk victims will never see.
- UltraMailer's own documentation describes rotating the chanret[.]com tracking domain to a private domain when it gets blocklisted, language that reads as explicit anti-blocklist guidance. The tool is openly promoted on sinister[.]li, patched[.]to, BreachForums, and Russian-language dark web platforms under titles like "UltraMailer: Best Spamming Tool In The Market." When Infoblox reported the campaign to Mail250, the account was suspended and the campaign stopped within days. The actor returned to chanret[.]com on September 8, 2026, because UltraMailer has no abuse-reporting mechanism on its website.
- A trojanized UltraMailer installer, UltraMailer_setup_v3.6_en.exe (SHA-256: 9e1a679ca45a149d2bd681cbb8ec3b1cc3d271fad51b092a3db5e5642eb6676b), carries an embedded njRAT payload, detected by 45 of 75 vendors on VirusTotal. The installer is unsigned but bundles an authentic UltraMailer copy signed with a DUC FABULOUS CO.,LTD Sectigo certificate (thumbprint 936BB9B6A2F8E1CD149B33F4A16D8A927CD675DE), meaning spammers hunting for the bulk-mail tool may themselves be getting backdoored.
- A trojanized UltraViewer installer, UltraViewer_setup_6.6.133_vi.exe (SHA-256: 28f046d9f985e58cbc8b245b54d4179feacecc12f41e2f6594306867ce3e8727), submitted to VirusTotal on September 4, 2026, was detected by 60 of 76 vendors and attributed to Win32.Comet.A, also known as DarkKometa. It drops its payload to C:\ProgramData\Synaptics\Synaptics.exe, impersonating the Synaptics touchpad driver. Third-party research by Hexastrike links the DUC FABULOUS CO.,LTD certificate used across these samples to the Chinese 🇨🇳 threat actor Silver Fox, though Infoblox could not independently confirm the certificate was stolen.
- Infoblox observed connections to ultraviewer[.]net from as many as 30% of their customers on some days, which reflects just how broadly this remote-access tool is deployed and how large the potential abuse surface is. qbcares[.]com is listed in the report as a QuickBooks lookalike example domain.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt your environment for Synaptics.exe running from C:\ProgramData\Synaptics\ as a process masquerading as a driver, and for outbound connections to track.chanret[.]com, ultraviewer[.]net, and ultramailer[.]org. Inspect email logs for GET requests containing base64-encoded addresses routed through chanret[.]com tracking pixels. Check endpoints for UltraViewer or UltraMailer installers signed with the DUC FABULOUS CO.,LTD certificate. The two SHA-256 hashes and additional IOCs are in the Infoblox report. If UltraViewer has no business justification in your environment, DNS or firewall blocks on ultraviewer[.]net will reduce the attack surface without waiting for an incident.

item.title: Hackers Exploited Cisco SD-WAN Flaw to Plant Malware Built to Steal Encryption Keys
item.description:
CVE-2026-20127 (CVSS 10.0): Custom malware KeyDrift planted on Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controllers to steal AES-256 encryption keys passing between routers, linked to infrastructure overlapping with Volt Typhoon activity.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-20127 is a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass affecting Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller (formerly vSmart), Manager (formerly vManage), and Validator (formerly vBond), on-premises and hosted, including FedRAMP environments. Exploitation allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to gain administrative privileges. Cisco confirmed limited exploitation in the wild. Volt Typhoon, per Lumen, was exploiting this flaw by late 2025 and continued after Cisco's February disclosure. No workaround eliminates the flaw; port-restricting 22 and 830 to known controller IPs is a partial interim measure only, and it does not remove malware already present.
- KeyDrift's architecture is purpose-built for key theft at the control plane. The component LittleFilch hooks into vdaemon, the process handling encrypted SD-WAN control connections, and reads control messages after decryption. It extracts IP addresses and a 32-byte field that Talos assesses is AES-256 key material, encrypts the collection with RSA, and writes it to /var/tmp/vdaemon.bin. A settings file at /var/tmp/vdaemon.conf specifies a UDP exfiltration destination and is deleted after a single read, which is why Talos could not recover it. Whether any keys were successfully exfiltrated is unknown.
- Persistence and injection follow a deliberate masquerade pattern. Modified runit scripts under /etc/sv/sshd/ launch the loader script conf_sshd before the real SSH server. conf_sshd writes vdaemon PIDs to /tmp/system-vdaemon, then rsshd injects PolyFlame (libdssl[.]so) into those processes. PolyFlame runs entirely in memory inside vdaemon and functions as a TinyShell-style backdoor and relay. It accepts commands embedded in SD-WAN control traffic and contains no hardcoded C2 address, complicating network-level detection. On Validators, a fake compiled binary aaamgrd under /etc/sv/aaamgr/ impersonates the real Python-based aaamgr component. The group also performed timestomping, copying timestamps and permissions from legitimate files onto malicious ones to blend modification times.
- Talos attributes this activity to UAT-11473, targeting space and satellite services, defense and aerospace, and policy research. Infrastructure "overlaps considerably" with Silent Train, the SOHO/IoT botnet Lumen associates with Volt Typhoon. Talos does not equate UAT-11473 with Volt Typhoon directly, and the relationship between UAT-11473 and UAT-8616 (the February exploitation cluster) is not stated. The Talos report does not include file hashes, domains, or IP IOCs for KeyDrift.
Practitioner takeaway: Start by checking /var/log/auth.log for "Accepted publickey for vmanage-admin" entries from unrecognized IPs, the exploitation indicator Cisco specifies. Run request admin-tech on each control component before opening a TAC case and re-scan those files using the Check Bug Applicability feature for bug CSCws52722. On compromised devices, audit /etc/sv/ for unexpected service directories (specifically /etc/sv/aaamgr/), inspect the run script under /etc/sv/sshd/ for conf_sshd references, and check for libdssl[.]so and libcommon[.]so. Because upgrading does not confirmed-clear existing implants and key replacement guidance is absent from Talos's advice, treat any positive finding as a full IR event. Talos released Snort rules 67387-67416 (Snort 2, disabled by default for subscriber sets) and 7:44-7:73 (Snort 3) for KeyDrift C2 detection on October 28. Rules 65938 and 65958 cover the CVE itself. US 🇺🇸 federal civilian agencies are under CISA's February 25 emergency directive: report root compromise to CISA and rebuild Controller, Manager, and Validator from patched images.

item.title: Hugging Face malware campaign returns to hijack GPUs for crypto mining
item.description:
Malicious Hugging Face model repositories return days after takedown, abusing trust_remote_code to deploy cryptominers and reverse shells on GPU inference servers, with one model reaching 28,412 downloads before removal.
Key findings:
- Pluto Security identified 31 malicious repositories across seven Hugging Face accounts, published in two waves since September. The models pose as Qwen2 test checkpoints and specifically target GPU hosts running self-hosted inference servers like Xinference and GPUStack. Rather than exploiting pickle deserialization or poisoned weights, the campaign abuses Hugging Face's trust_remote_code option, which executes a model's bundled Python code the moment a user loads it. Code runs before any model inference begins, so the attacker foothold is established silently at load time.
- The primary payload installs a cryptocurrency miner disguised as a Linux system process, includes a watchdog that restarts it if killed, and evicts competing miners from the machine. Some variants also open a reverse shell for direct attacker access. A model pushed hours after the first-wave takedown added a container escape script capable of taking over the underlying host. The operator's wallet received roughly $5,000 in Pearl (PRL) cryptocurrency, and the mining infrastructure was still active on pools after the repositories were removed.
- A second wave of 19 repositories appeared within days under new accounts. The flagship model scanned clean through Hugging Face's antivirus and partner tooling from Protect AI and JFrog, collecting 28,412 downloads while evading detection. A near-identical copy uploaded October 25 by account htt0118 was still live at time of reporting and BleepingComputer confirmed it carries the same miner and reverse shell. Pluto attributes the campaign to a financially motivated, Chinese 🇨🇳 speaking operator based on Simplified Chinese 🇨🇳 code comments, C2 infrastructure on Alibaba Cloud, and activity timing consistent with late-night hours in China 🇨🇳.
- Separately, Air Security flagged GitHub repository SolanaUpdateTools/solana-starter-kit, live since November 2025 with 286 stars, that positions itself as a top AI coding agent search result for Solana development. Its README contains a single PowerShell one-liner that assembles a URL from fragments at developer-update[.]app and fetches a script into memory. That script installs NetSupport Manager configured to beacon to maxwintodaybtc[.]com and establishes persistence at every login. A fake error message tells the user or agent to retry in 72 hours, designed to pass as a routine service hiccup. Air links this to a known NetSupport RAT operator previously tracked by eSentire.
Takeaway: Any system that loaded a Hugging Face model with trust_remote_code enabled in the last several months should be treated as fully compromised, not merely mined. Killing the miner process is insufficient. Hunt for unexpected processes masquerading as Linux system services, outbound connections to mining pools, and unauthorized reverse shell activity. Check for container escape artifacts if the host runs a shared GPU cluster. Rotate all credentials that machine could have accessed. For the Solana kit exposure, look for NetSupport Manager persistence and outbound connections to maxwintodaybtc[.]com. IOCs for both campaigns are in Pluto's and Air Security's respective reports.

item.title: VAPOR PANDA Uses AI-Driven ARTEX to Scale a Global Espionage Campaign
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 APT VAPOR PANDA weaponizes the ARTEX agentic AI framework alongside DeepSeek to hit 200+ organizations across 14 countries in 11 days, deploying the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor and scaling espionage at a pace no manual operation could match.
Key details:
- Starting October 17, 2026, a single ARTEX controller linked to VAPOR PANDA infrastructure directed simultaneous intrusions against foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East; 19 U.S. 🇺🇸 organizations spanning pharma, semiconductor, defense, nuclear, and finance; and telecom providers in the U.S. 🇺🇸, Belgium 🇧🇪, and the Philippines 🇵🇭. CrowdStrike OverWatch confirmed post-exploitation at nine organizations. ARTEX transcripts recovered from an inadvertently exposed controller show the operator issuing instructions in Chinese 🇨🇳, timestamped in China 🇨🇳 Standard Time, labeled 【人类指令】 ("human instruction"), with commands to write web shells, extract domain admin passwords, and map endpoint sensor coverage.
- The attack chains were multi-path and adaptive. At one U.S. 🇺🇸 pharma org, the agent chained an unsigned SAML assertion (T1606.002) with an XXE flaw (T1190) to query the cloud Instance Metadata Service (T1552.005), obtaining a role with command-execution reach over thousands of instances. At a second pharma org, the agent deployed web shells (T1505.003), abused an unauthenticated orchestration service for container root access, read LAPS passwords (T1555), and used resource-based constrained delegation to impersonate a privileged account (T1134.001). Against a Greek 🇬🇷 government entity, the operator fed the agent a 2022 mail server directory export containing unrotated authentication keys; the agent forged an admin token (T1606), read mailboxes (T1114.002), and pivoted internally via leaked VPN configs (T1078, T1133). Planning agents consumed roughly 1.4 billion input tokens in a single intrusion, indicating enormous automated throughput across the full operation.
- BLOODALCHEMY, a backdoor first documented in October 2023, was deployed at a Middle East-based interior ministry and a Latin America-based foreign ministry. Delivery used DLL hijacking (T1574.001): a legitimate GameHook binary was renamed svchost.exe (T1036.005) to load graphics-hook-filter64.dll, which decrypted the payload graphics-hook_config.bin. The implant's internal project path is D:\ProjectX\Merman_New\. C2 domains: nginxmysql[.]com (45.153.126[.]223), sqlserver-sqlite[.]com (89.46.234[.]50), www.ddduuuppp[.]com (192.121.47[.]20). Hashes for all three files are in the IOC table in the report. C2 traffic was routed through Tor, SOCKS proxies, and a compromised relay (T1090.003), and tunneled via Chisel and SoftEther (T1572).
- Sensor evasion was baked directly into the agentic workflow. The operator instructed agents to "find Windows machines in the domain without Falcon, judging by tasklist and folder listings" (T1518.001), using 猎鹰, PRC red-team slang for the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor. This means unprotected hosts are being systematically identified and prioritized for follow-on activity at machine speed, not discovered opportunistically by a human operator.
Practitioner takeaway: hunt for ARTEX artifacts directly. The report specifies: command-line parameters containing artx or artex strings, artx-prefixed cloud role names, art18- administration-command comments in cloud logs, and the directory C:\ProgramData\artx5v\. Also audit for the BLOODALCHEMY triad: svchost.exe with a hash mismatch against the legitimate binary, graphics-hook-filter64.dll, and graphics-hook_config.bin in the same path. Rotate any signing keys, preauthentication keys, or service credentials that appeared in historical directory exports or backup data, including keys from 2022 or earlier. Enforce SAML signature validation and IMDSv2 now. IOCs and the full ATT&CK technique table are in the CrowdStrike report.

item.content:encoded:
Chinese 🇨🇳 APT VAPOR PANDA weaponizes the ARTEX agentic AI framework alongside DeepSeek to hit 200+ organizations across 14 countries in 11 days, deploying the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor and scaling espionage at a pace no manual operation could match.

Key details:

- Starting October 17, 2026, a single ARTEX controller linked to VAPOR PANDA infrastructure directed simultaneous intrusions against foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East; 19 U.S. 🇺🇸 organizations spanning pharma, semiconductor, defense, nuclear, and finance; and telecom providers in the U.S. 🇺🇸, Belgium 🇧🇪, and the Philippines 🇵🇭. CrowdStrike OverWatch confirmed post-exploitation at nine organizations. ARTEX transcripts recovered from an inadvertently exposed controller show the operator issuing instructions in Chinese 🇨🇳, timestamped in China 🇨🇳 Standard Time, labeled 【人类指令】 ("human instruction"), with commands to write web shells, extract domain admin passwords, and map endpoint sensor coverage.

- The attack chains were multi-path and adaptive. At one U.S. 🇺🇸 pharma org, the agent chained an unsigned SAML assertion (T1606.002) with an XXE flaw (T1190) to query the cloud Instance Metadata Service (T1552.005), obtaining a role with command-execution reach over thousands of instances. At a second pharma org, the agent deployed web shells (T1505.003), abused an unauthenticated orchestration service for container root access, read LAPS passwords (T1555), and used resource-based constrained delegation to impersonate a privileged account (T1134.001). Against a Greek 🇬🇷 government entity, the operator fed the agent a 2022 mail server directory export containing unrotated authentication keys; the agent forged an admin token (T1606), read mailboxes (T1114.002), and pivoted internally via leaked VPN configs (T1078, T1133). Planning agents consumed roughly 1.4 billion input tokens in a single intrusion, indicating enormous automated throughput across the full operation.

- BLOODALCHEMY, a backdoor first documented in October 2023, was deployed at a Middle East-based interior ministry and a Latin America-based foreign ministry. Delivery used DLL hijacking (T1574.001): a legitimate GameHook binary was renamed svchost.exe (T1036.005) to load graphics-hook-filter64.dll, which decrypted the payload graphics-hook_config.bin. The implant's internal project path is D:\ProjectX\Merman_New\. C2 domains: nginxmysql[.]com (45.153.126[.]223), sqlserver-sqlite[.]com (89.46.234[.]50), www.ddduuuppp[.]com (192.121.47[.]20). Hashes for all three files are in the IOC table in the report. C2 traffic was routed through Tor, SOCKS proxies, and a compromised relay (T1090.003), and tunneled via Chisel and SoftEther (T1572).

- Sensor evasion was baked directly into the agentic workflow. The operator instructed agents to "find Windows machines in the domain without Falcon, judging by tasklist and folder listings" (T1518.001), using 猎鹰, PRC red-team slang for the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor. This means unprotected hosts are being systematically identified and prioritized for follow-on activity at machine speed, not discovered opportunistically by a human operator.

Practitioner takeaway: hunt for ARTEX artifacts directly. The report specifies: command-line parameters containing artx or artex strings, artx-prefixed cloud role names, art18- administration-command comments in cloud logs, and the directory C:\ProgramData\artx5v\. Also audit for the BLOODALCHEMY triad: svchost.exe with a hash mismatch against the legitimate binary, graphics-hook-filter64.dll, and graphics-hook_config.bin in the same path. Rotate any signing keys, preauthentication keys, or service credentials that appeared in historical directory exports or backup data, including keys from 2022 or earlier. Enforce SAML signature validation and IMDSv2 now. IOCs and the full ATT&CK technique table are in the CrowdStrike report.

item.title: Volt Typhoon targeted enterprise control planes via ever-changing “Silent Train” relay network
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 Volt Typhoon's "Silent Train" relay network targeted control plane infrastructure across US 🇺🇸 critical sectors using zero-days, in-memory webshells, and log erasure to minimize forensic trace.
Key findings:
- Silent Train is a covert, transient relay network built from more than 27 device classes, including TP-Link, Netgear, Zyxel, Ruckus, and Cambium SOHO/IoT gear as early hops, and Fortinet, Cisco, PRTG, Mirth Connect, and CyberPanel as final hops before the victim. Sessions originate from VPS nodes outside the US 🇺🇸, pass through overseas compromised devices, and exit through US-based nodes before hitting the target, blending traffic to bypass geo-blocking and IP reputation filters. Up to six hops separated the operator from the victim.
- The zero-days and known CVEs exploited through Silent Train against control plane systems include CVE-2024-39717 (Versa Director), CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876 (N-Able N-Central), CVE-2026-20127 (Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN), CVE-2026-16812 (VeloCloud Orchestrator), and a suspected unknown zero-day against Quest KACE. Targeting SD-WAN orchestrators and endpoint management platforms gave the group native administrative reach across victim networks without requiring lateral movement.
- Post-incident forensics with partners found in-memory webshells (leaving no on-disk artifact), credential harvesting, abuse of native endpoint control and remote file transfer features, and deliberate log erasure or alteration. The Cisco Talos report on UAT-11473, whose infrastructure overlaps considerably with Silent Train, details a custom malware framework called KeyDrift deployed on Cisco SD-WAN Catalyst Controllers to maintain persistent access and exfiltrate control-session metadata and data-plane keying material.
- Infrastructure evolved after the December 2023 KV botnet takedown: Volt Typhoon shifted from SSH-chaining through SOHO/IoT devices toward reverse-tunnel variants using open-source proxies Chisel and FRP, mixing models to avoid the recurring patterns that made the KV botnet detectable. Each Silent Train session was short-lived, with SOHO devices often wiped and restored after a single use, leaving a narrow forensic window.
- Victimology over three years spans US 🇺🇸 federal entities, telecoms, defense contractors, satellite and mission-critical communications providers, MSPs, military-affiliated universities, and critical infrastructure in water, energy, transportation, aviation, and emergency services. Hawaii, California, and Texas were the most targeted states, consistent with pre-positioning for potential disruption of Indo-Pacific-relevant military and logistics networks.
DFIR takeaway: The in-memory webshell and log-tampering combination means disk-based triage will under-report this activity. On compromised control plane systems (Versa Director, N-Central, Cisco SD-WAN controllers), prioritize volatile memory acquisition over disk imaging. Look for anomalous administrative actions (mass credential pulls, unexpected remote file transfers, config exports) in whatever audit or syslog telemetry survived before log erasure. On network edge gear acting as relay nodes, examine connection-state tables and process lists for Chisel or FRP reverse-tunnel processes, and correlate short-lived external SSH sessions with outbound tunnel establishment. IOCs and additional campaign detail are in the Black Lotus Labs report and the Cisco Talos post on UAT-11473.

item.title: Hackers exploit Cisco SD-WAN flaw to deploy custom KeyDrift malware
item.description:
APT group UAT-11473, linked to Volt Typhoon, is exploiting a max-severity Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN auth-bypass to deploy KeyDrift, a framework built to silently steal IPsec encryption keys from network control-plane traffic.
Key details:
- CVE-2026-20127 is a max-severity authentication-bypass in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controllers and Manager, patched in February 2026. UAT-8616 exploited it as a zero-day from at least 2023, and UAT-11473 overlaps with Volt Typhoon's "Silent Train" covert access network per Cisco Talos, though no definitive attribution link has been confirmed. Targets include space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research organizations.
- KeyDrift has two components, PolyFlame and LittleFilch, both showing signs of active development including new anti-debugging mechanisms and process impersonation. PolyFlame runs inside legitimate vdaemon processes via modified service startup scripts and an injector, supports command execution through a TinyShell-styled component, and relays C2 communications across peers. LittleFilch hooks SSL_read inside the controller to intercept decrypted control-plane messages and extract IP identifiers plus 32-byte AES-256 IPsec data-plane key material, which it RSA-encrypts and writes to /var/tmp/vdaemon.bin before transmitting over UDP.
- The forensic risk here is not just initial access but cryptographic compromise. If KeyDrift successfully exfiltrated keying material, any traffic encrypted with those IPsec keys is potentially retrospectively readable. Incident responders should treat IPsec key material across affected SD-WAN deployments as compromised and initiate re-keying across the entire data-plane fabric.
- Detection opportunities center on process anomalies inside vdaemon, unexpected modifications to service startup scripts, the presence of /var/tmp/vdaemon.bin, and anomalous outbound UDP from SD-WAN controller nodes. Unauthorized peer additions in the Controller and Manager interface are also an indicator of post-exploitation activity enabled by the auth-bypass itself.
Responder action: audit vdaemon process trees on all Catalyst SD-WAN controllers for injected children or modified startup scripts, and check /var/tmp/ for vdaemon.bin. Treat any positive finding as full key compromise and rotate IPsec keying material before trusting the network fabric. Apply Cisco's CVE-2026-20127 patch and consult the vendor's Catalyst SD-WAN hardening guide.

item.title: The Quiet Phase: Why Active Directory Group Enumeration Deserves Your Attention
item.description:
Active Directory group enumeration is the quiet phase attackers exploit before privilege escalation, and most teams have no visibility into it whatsoever.
Key findings:
- The core gap: alerting on Domain Admins membership changes catches attackers after the breach. Event 4662 (An operation was performed on an object) and Event 4799 catch them during reconnaissance, days or weeks earlier, when they still hold only low-privilege access. MITRE tracks this as T1069.002 (Permission Groups Discovery: Domain Groups). Tools like SharpHound, PowerView, and native ActiveDirectory PowerShell cmdlets gather this in minutes using any authenticated account.
- Two prerequisites must both be in place or the logging silently fails. First, enable Audit Directory Service Access (Success) under Advanced Audit Policy > DS Access via GPO on the Domain Controllers OU. For built-in groups, also enable Audit Security Group Management (Success) under Account Management. Second, add a SACL to every group you care about: Everyone, Success, This object only, Read member (attribute GUID bf9679c0-0de6-11d0-a285-00aa003049e2). The report includes the exact PowerShell to set both. Without the SACL, the policy is meaningless. AdminSDHolder needs the SACL too, because adminCount=1 groups like Domain Admins and Enterprise Admins are reset from it every 60 minutes, wiping any directly applied audit rule.
- Event 4662 does not record the source IP or workstation. To recover those, join the event's SubjectLogonId to the TargetLogonId of a 4624 logon event on the same domain controller. That join is your pivot to identify the machine to isolate. Events are only logged on the DC that answered the query, so any DC missing the audit policy is a blind spot an attacker can exploit without knowing it. SAMR-based tools like net group /domain bypass the LDAP-based 4662 signal entirely, so cover that path separately: Event 4688 or Sysmon Event 1 for net.exe and net1.exe, and network-level detection of the SAMR RPC interface over SMB.
- Honeypot groups are the high-confidence layer. A decoy group with a realistic name (think Tier0-Server-Admins or SQL-Prod-Admins), one or two fake members with SPNs to bait Kerberoasting (Event 4769), and a SACL auditing all property reads produces near-zero noise. Any 4662 against it is a true positive. When the same SubjectLogonId reads the decoy and real admin groups within minutes, you are watching a SharpHound-style collector in real time. That correlation is the alert worth paging someone over.
- Log volume planning is not optional. Every SACL on every group generates events on every DC that serves reads. Baseline legitimate readers (Entra Connect, Exchange, PAM platforms, inventory tools, ADUC) for a month before alerting on production groups. Build allowlists in the SIEM so the raw evidence stays in the Security log for forensic use while analysts see only the signal. The report's phased rollout is: audit policy everywhere first, one or two honeypot groups with SIEM alert second, baseline and filter for a month third, then extend SACLs to Tier 0 groups via AdminSDHolder.
Practitioner takeaway: TrustedSec released QuietPhase, a PowerShell script at github[.]com/d3lightfu1/QuietPhase that audits your current posture, checks SACLs on Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Schema Admins, Key Admins, Group Policy Creator Owners, Builtin operator groups, and AdminSDHolder, flags gaps as NeedsChange, and exports ready-to-paste remediation. Run it report-only first with -AllDomainControllers, then test in a lab by running SharpHound or PowerView from a test account and confirming 4662 and 4799 events fire before touching production.

item.title: Polymarket Breach Alert: Wallet-Draining Code Found in a Third-Party Script
item.description:
Wallet-draining JavaScript found inside a DebugBear performance-monitoring script served to Polymarket users, with build metadata confirming removal and one user reporting $800,000 stolen on October 29, 2026.
Key findings:
- Hudson Rock retrieved cdn.debugbear[.]com/C7xcKKrjUnXK.js twice on October 29 at 18:12:06 and 18:13:04 UTC. Both downloads returned identical 15,187-byte payloads with SHA-256 0755e767504d8103f6c27b9e765a1026507a17c04513242adb503df7777879e5. The script reads three localStorage entries: polymarket.auth.params, polymarket.auth.proxyWallet, and poly_clob_api_key_map, then traverses React component internals to locate a live trading client exposing postOrder, createOrder, or createMarketOrder. It does not exfiltrate seed phrases or private keys; it reuses authority already present in the authenticated session to submit orders and sign EIP-712 DepositWallet batch transfers on Polygon.
- The payload branches on account type. For EOA accounts it constructs an ERC-1155 batch transfer directly to a hard-coded fallback recipient: 0x3F99139F1C5854bb628c2e576Aaf638e99dFfc18. For Magic and non-EOA accounts it first attempts SELL orders at escalating prices, then moves proceeds. Theft is conditional on account state, signer availability, and relayer response, so not every exposed session necessarily lost funds. A configuration check to /metrics/init returned HTTP 404, meaning the script fell back to built-in settings including that recipient address.
- Reporting paths encoded in the sample are data.debugbear[.]com/metrics/submit, data.debugbear[.]com/metrics/update, and data.debugbear[.]com/metrics/handle. Fields sent include wallet addresses, IP, country, OS, account type, portfolio values, and transfer-result fields. A tracking UUID 4c6b64a0-a7ef-4c0f-9c70-3a4e6f89065c appears in the configuration and reporting logic. No reporting requests were executed in the review.
- Polymarket's own production build metadata, retrieved at 18:13:43 UTC from a first-party application asset (SHA-256 01c5bc78c4118115bd849ad34e3c42d7ff39479a0feb5b216b1e1ffdc02f853d), carries the change message "chore(polymarket): remove debugbear rum script (#15337)" with build timestamp 2026-10-29T17:59:20.443Z and commit f908fe564ea73067b09ab1f0c5d683970020fbca. The homepage captured at that same moment showed no DebugBear script reference in the page or its Content Security Policy. Build timestamp is not verified deployment or containment time: cached tabs, previously authenticated sessions, and dynamically imported code remain outside that scope.
- Reported impact is $800,000 from a single user ([@]CarOnPolymarket), whose follow-up post states all positions were sold. The fallback recipient address held approximately $2.19 million in POL and token holdings per a PolygonScan screenshot, though that balance cannot be treated as a verified theft total independent of the loss report. The initial compromise vector, exact exposure window, number of affected users, and aggregate losses remain unresolved. A prior June 25, 2026 incident involving approximately $3 million is a separate event.
Practitioner takeaway: The forensic priority right now is evidence preservation before CDN responses change. Capture the exact response bytes, HTTP headers, and hash for any cached or logged copy of cdn.debugbear[.]com/C7xcKKrjUnXK.js. For affected-user triage, review browser localStorage for the three polymarket.auth keys, examine local browser history and network logs for requests to the three /metrics/ paths at data.debugbear[.]com, and pull on-chain activity at the fallback recipient address to trace timing of inbound transfers. For application teams, this case is a direct argument for Subresource Integrity on every third-party script loaded into an authenticated signing context: a trusted CDN hostname provides no verification of the bytes it actually serves. IOCs and evidence details are in the report.

For affected-user triage, review browser localStorage for the three polymarket.auth keys, examine local browser history and network logs for requests to the three /metrics/ paths at data.debugbear[.]com, and pull on-chain activity at the fallback recipient address to trace timing of inbound transfers. For application teams, this case is a direct argument for Subresource Integrity on every third-party script loaded into an authenticated signing context: a trusted CDN hostname provides no verification of the bytes it actually serves. IOCs and evidence details are in the report.

item.title: Malicious Firefox extensions impersonate popular crypto wallets
item.description:
Three malicious Firefox extensions impersonated Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget crypto wallets, harvesting recovery phrases and private keys and automatically draining funds across nine blockchain networks.
Key findings:
- The extensions (Firefox Add-on IDs 3092199, 3092666, and 3092059) were listed on the official Firefox Add-ons store and accepted as legitimate listings. All three have since been removed, but any browser where they remain installed should be treated as compromised. The fake Phantom listing requested access to data on all websites and carried no privacy policy, two red flags that apply broadly when vetting any browser extension.
- The credential-harvesting logic targeted 12-, 15-, 18-, and 24-word recovery phrases and both Ethereum and Solana private keys. The extensions could read input fields, detect pasted text, and scan screens where a recovery phrase was displayed, meaning a victim was exposed whether they typed the phrase, pasted it, or simply viewed a reveal screen inside the extension UI.
- The Phantom impersonator was the most developed variant. It logged captured secrets, forwarded them to a Telegram bot for real-time attacker notification, and then executed automated fund sweeps to hardcoded payout addresses covering Ethereum, BSC, Polygon, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, Avalanche, Solana, and Bitcoin. The automation matters because there is no detection window between exfiltration and loss.
- The infrastructure behind all three extensions centers on bonto[.]io, with subdomains phantom.bonto[.]io, jupiter.bonto[.]io, bitget.bonto[.]io, coinbase.bonto[.]io, and exodus.bonto[.]io indicating the operator built out additional impersonation capability beyond the three published extensions. Associated IPs are 104.21.34[.]69 and 172.67.155[.]198.
Responder takeaway: if you are investigating a crypto drain on a Firefox user's machine, check the browser extension directory for Add-on IDs 3092199, 3092666, or 3092059 before anything else. Extension persistence in Firefox lives under the browser profile folder in extensions.json and the extensions subdirectory. Treat any wallet the victim used with that browser as fully compromised regardless of whether they recall entering a phrase, because the extensions monitored paste and screen-reveal events silently. Block bonto[.]io and its subdomains at the network layer. If a phrase was exposed, the only recovery path is creating a new wallet on a clean device and moving assets immediately. The old wallet is gone.

item.title: Extracting Timestamps from ChatGPT IDs
item.description:
ChatGPT conversation URLs contain an embedded Unix timestamp in every UUIDv8 ID generated since 2024-08-30, extractable from the URL string alone without ever accessing the conversation.
Key findings:
- Every ChatGPT conversation URL created from 2024-08-30 onward uses a UUIDv8 where the first 8 hex characters are a plain big-endian Unix timestamp (seconds). Decode hex chars 0-7 as a 32-bit integer and you have the conversation creation time in UTC. Validated across 180k+ IDs against Wayback Machine capture times: the embedded time preceded first capture in the vast majority of cases, with a median gap of 71 seconds. The URL does not need to be reachable for this to work, so it is valid on dead links, private conversations, and evidence collected from browser history or proxy logs.
- Pre-2024-08-30 conversation IDs are UUIDv4 (random, no timestamp), but that version difference is itself a forensic signal: a UUIDv4 conversation ID establishes the chat was created before the August 30 cutoff. The rollout was a node 6 canary from 2024-08-30 to 2024-09-02, then all 20 nodes live by 2024-09-04. Node values in the ID (hex chars 13-15) also correlate with rough date ranges, giving an independent consistency check.
- The same 128-bit structure (timestamp, sub-second field, version 8, node, random) appears across the ChatGPT and OpenAI surface: shared conversation links at chatgpt[.]com/share/ and chatgpt[.]com/s/, Custom GPTs at chatgpt[.]com/g/, Codex task IDs (task_e_, task_b_, task_i_ prefixes), Sora 2 posts at sora.chatgpt[.]com/p/s_, OpenAI API objects (vs_, batch_, eval_, resp_, msg_ prefixes), and notification IDs in query parameters. A 32-hex-character string with the right layout carries a creation timestamp almost anywhere it appears in OpenAI infrastructure.
- OpenAI Chat Completions API IDs (chatcmpl- followed by 29 alphanumeric characters) use a separate scheme: read the first 5 characters as a base62 number and add 1,576,800,000 (2019-12-20 00:00:00 UTC) to get the Unix creation time. Validated against 152 public API responses: 150 of 152 matched (138 exact, 12 off by one second). These IDs appear as image file names when API-generated images are published to the web, so file names in evidence can be decoded for a creation timestamp without any API access.
- Sora generation and task links (sora[.]com/g/gen_..., sora.chatgpt[.]com/t/task_...) use 26-character ULIDs where the first 10 characters are a millisecond-precision timestamp. None of roughly 2,350 archived IDs had a time later than first capture. Earliest archived generation ID dates to 2024-11-19, about three weeks before Sora's public launch.
Practitioner takeaway: When ChatGPT URLs appear in browser history, proxy logs, phishing redirect chains, or chat logs, extract the UUID from the /c/ path and decode hex chars 0-7 as a big-endian Unix timestamp. That gives you conversation creation time to the second, independent of whether the URL resolves. Unfurl (dfir-unfurl, updated in v2026.11) handles all of the formats described above automatically, including bare UUIDs that pass strict false-positive checks. Bare undashed 32-hex strings are more prone to misfire; the report recommends requiring dashes when no chatgpt[.]com URL context is present.
