item.title: AI, Scripts, Operator: Inside the ConnectWise Attack
item.description:
Storm-0940 abused compromised ConnectWise cloud backup credentials to hit more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, reaching Global Administrator in under three hours, with behavioral evidence pointing to an AI agent adapting the tooling mid-operation.
Key findings:
- The attack chain ran in three modes on October 15: scripted loops fired token requests against nearly 1,000 tenants in ascending tenant ID order using Python-urllib/3.12 from 144.172.64[.]128, a thread pool burst 100 requests in under 10 seconds at 13 to 21 attempts per second, and a pilot-then-batch pattern tested actions in one tenant before batching them, a sequence observed three times across two tools. The password spray phase, October 10 to 14, originated from 144.172.64[.]99 and 194.165.16[.]21. Entry came via compromised ConnectWise application credentials (T1078.004, T1199), bypassing any per-user authentication entirely.
- The strongest behavioral signal for an agent in the loop came at 03:48:24 UTC: a certificate upload failed on a thumbprint mismatch with no retry. Fifty-five seconds later the next run added exponential backoff retry logic (3.5 seconds, then 7.1 seconds) that had not existed before, and carried it into a second tenant 47 seconds after that. A script does not rewrite itself between runs. Huntress rates LLM involvement at low-to-medium on their telemetry alone, rising to medium-to-high when Microsoft's attribution to Storm-0940 using ARTEX (T1588.007) is factored in. ARTEX is an open-source multi-agent framework that builds an asset graph and runs parallel breach paths from recon through exfiltration with minimal human interaction.
- Privilege escalation (T1098.003) used the Teams service principal to assign itself Global Administrator via Microsoft Graph, then granted elevated roles to sibling service principals when a removal failed. Credential persistence (T1098.001) involved adding secrets and uploading certificates to victim application identities. A critical visibility gap: Microsoft Graph reads are not recorded in Entra audit logs, and no known victim had Graph activity logging enabled, so the full scope of data access cannot be reconstructed from available logs. Application-only audit events also carry no source IP, making some credential changes untraceable to a specific address.
- The operation was clumsy but effective: secrets were added and removed and added again, a certificate failed, and single-tenant app secrets were replayed against a hundred tenants where they could never work. Despite that, the stolen application credential compressed the attack from targeting to privileged access across multiple environments in under three hours. The user agent strings show deliberate manipulation (T1036): python-requests/2.31 instead of the library default python-requests/2.31.0, and a browser string missing its standard "(KHTML, like Gecko)" segment, both consistent with a model generating strings from memory rather than copying them from a live library.
Practitioner takeaway: The detections that held here will not hold long. Cadence and retry timing were the most useful signals in this investigation, and a better tool will normalize them away. Focus on what the activity does, not how it looks. Alert on any service principal assigning itself Global Administrator or Privileged Role Administrator (T1098.003), credential additions to high-privilege applications from unexpected sources (T1098.001), and any vendor application deviating from its baseline user agent, the clearest early signal was kiota-dotnet being replaced by Python-urllib/3.12. Storm-0940 abused compromised ConnectWise cloud backup credentials to hit more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, reaching Global Administrator in under three hours, with behavioral evidence pointing to an AI agent adapting the tooling mid-operation.

Key findings:

- The attack chain ran in three modes on October 15: scripted loops fired token requests against nearly 1,000 tenants in ascending tenant ID order using Python-urllib/3.12 from 144.172.64[.]128, a thread pool burst 100 requests in under 10 seconds at 13 to 21 attempts per second, and a pilot-then-batch pattern tested actions in one tenant before batching them, a sequence observed three times across two tools. The password spray phase, October 10 to 14, originated from 144.172.64[.]99 and 194.165.16[.]21. Entry came via compromised ConnectWise application credentials (T1078.004, T1199), bypassing any per-user authentication entirely.

Fifty-five seconds later the next run added exponential backoff retry logic (3.5 seconds, then 7.1 seconds) that had not existed before, and carried it into a second tenant 47 seconds after that. A script does not rewrite itself between runs. Huntress rates LLM involvement at low-to-medium on their telemetry alone, rising to medium-to-high when Microsoft's attribution to Storm-0940 using ARTEX (T1588.007) is factored in. ARTEX is an open-source multi-agent framework that builds an asset graph and runs parallel breach paths from recon through exfiltration with minimal human interaction.

item.title: Attackers Use Microsoft Teams IT Support Scams to Deploy Malware and Ransomware
item.description:
Microsoft Teams external chat is the new phishing lure: hundreds of cases share the same IT-impersonation playbook, ending in RMM abuse, backdoor deployment, and Chaos ransomware.
Key findings:
- The attack chain opens with mail bombing, flooding the target inbox with newsletter confirmations to manufacture urgency, then a Teams message arrives from an external tenant using IT-themed display names like "IT Support (Internal)", "HelpDesk Supervisor", or "Enterprise IT & Security (Internal)". Attackers now add the victim organization's own domain or company name to the display name to defeat the external-user warning banner. Between 30-40% of cases use *.onmicrosoft[.]com tenant names such as helpdeskteam365.onmicrosoft[.]com, itendpoint365.onmicrosoft[.]com, itcoreportal.onmicrosoft[.]com, and itadmin922.onmicrosoft[.]com. Roughly 50% of paid-TLD variants use .top, consistent with STAC4749 tradecraft previously linked to Chaos ransomware by Sophos.
- Once the victim engages, vishing moves them to grant remote hands-on-keyboard access via legitimate RMM tools: Quick Assist, AnyDesk, ScreenConnect, TeamViewer, Atera, Zoho Assist, NetSupport, or LogMeIn. The remote session is then used to navigate directly to payload URLs, deliberately bypassing Safe Links and ZAP scanning by avoiding pasting URLs into Teams chat itself.
- In documented cases, the attacker instructs the user to run a PowerShell command that pulls an MSI installer from Microsoft Azure Blob Storage. That installer launches a PowerShell script which extracts and executes a Python implant. The implant then runs a second MSI transaction issuing LDAP queries to Active Directory for all computer and user objects and exfiltrates the results externally. A second payload, the GoGRPC backdoor, has also been observed alongside the RMM tool Level deployed for redundant access before lateral movement to domain controllers and final ransomware staging.
- Attackers deliberately avoid pasting URLs into Teams to evade message-scanning controls, instead navigating to payloads themselves during the remote session. Arctic Wolf notes that endpoint and identity telemetry are the essential monitoring surfaces here, not message scanning alone. Microsoft's built-in Notes feature within Teams has also been observed as a delivery mechanism for attacker content in a subset of cases.
Practitioner takeaway: prioritize endpoint and identity telemetry over message-scanning for this vector. Hunt for RMM tool installations (Quick Assist, AnyDesk, ScreenConnect, Level) preceded by Teams external chat activity in your collaboration logs, then pivot to PowerShell spawning msiexec with arguments pointing to Azure Blob Storage URLs. Review Entra ID / Azure AD sign-in logs for newly created external tenants with .onmicrosoft[.]com or .top domains initiating chat sessions. If your organization does not require external Teams chat, disable it at the tenant level. IOCs and infrastructure patterns are detailed in the Arctic Wolf Labs report.

item.title: Looking for a Language [Guest Diary], (Wed, Oct 21st)
item.description:
HTTP Accept-Language and Accept-Charset headers in web honeypot logs expose automated scanning campaigns, including hosts in Canadian 🇨🇦 AS space broadcasting Mainland Chinese 🇨🇳 character set preferences while probing internet-facing endpoints.
Key findings:
- A DShield SIEM honeypot on a Raspberry Pi collected roughly 960,000 log records across just over 3 weeks, yet only 15,271 triggered any detection rule. The remaining 944,000-plus records went unruled, which is exactly the gap this analysis targets. The method is iterative feature selection: use Kibana Field Statistics to find fields with low distinct-value counts (Distribution 2 to 6), eliminate fields that are uniform across all records, and home in on the outlier values that demand explanation.
- The pivot started with the http.request.mime_type field, where a subset of records sent the Accept-Charset value "GBK,utf-8;q=0.7,*;q=0.3". GBK is the Simplified Chinese 🇨🇳 character set extension of GB 2312. Finding that preference explicitly declared in requests hitting a non-Chinese honeypot was the first anomaly. Filtering on that exact string narrowed 960,000 records to 47.
- Geolocation on those 47 records showed two source regions: Beijing (expected) and Ontario (not expected). The Ontario traffic traced to AS-7456. Pivoting on that autonomous system number and running the same distribution analysis revealed that all 31 records with an explicit Accept-Language header declared zh-CN as their primary language preference, either "zh-CN,zh;q=0.9,en;q=0.8,en-GB;q=0.7,en-US;q=0.6" or "zh-CN,zh;q=0.8". No attempt was made to suppress or rotate these headers.
- The 6 source IPs tied to AS-7456 were 165.154.36[.]91, 165.154.29[.]93, 165.154.11[.]140, 165.154.120[.]226, 165.154.33[.]72, and 165.154.182[.]221. Their request bodies cycled through /cgi-bin/login, /config.json, /sitemap.xml, /robots.txt, /favicon.ico, and /. Associated domains extracted via ESQL include tzrhxln[.]cn (flagged as high-entropy), leheedu[.]cn, mail.brossy[.]com[.]cn, and a malformed variant of the same. All resolve within AS-7456 and all show strong CN presence.
Practitioner takeaway: in your web proxy or honeypot logs, filter on http.request.accept-language values beginning with "zh-CN" or http.request.mime_type values containing "GBK" originating outside China 🇨🇳. Cross-reference with source AS number rather than raw IP, since VPS infrastructure rotates addresses frequently but AS attribution is stickier. The ESQL query pattern used to extract source.domain values from the filtered record set is described in the report and is straightforward to replicate against any Elastic index with HTTP header fields populated.

item.title: Microsoft 365 Token-Replay Attacks Compromise 97 Accounts at 79 Organizations
item.description:
Microsoft 365 token-replay campaign hit 79 organizations, compromising 97 accounts by replaying stolen session tokens at scale, bypassing MFA entirely, and planting rogue Entra devices for durable persistence.
Key findings:
- Huntress tracked the campaign from July 14 to September 22, 2026, observing over 200,000 login attempts that produced 497 successful Microsoft 365 sign-ins. The attacker used an adversary-in-the-middle relay to capture credentials, MFA codes, and the resulting access tokens from victims mid-session, then replayed those tokens from attacker-controlled infrastructure within minutes. Huntress calls the technique "token spraying," a scaled, multi-org version of token replay analogous to password spraying. The bulk of failed attempts trace back to the 193.26.115[.]0/24 IP range, hosted by 1337 Services GmbH, a German 🇩🇪 VPS provider linked to StarkRDP and rdp[.]sh, now rebranded as exy[.]sh.
- Once inside, attackers moved fast on persistence. In at least 19 organizations, victim MFA methods were removed and a rogue authenticator registered within three hours of first access. In one July 21 session, an authenticator app named "iPhone 13" was added less than 51 minutes after token hijack. Beyond MFA manipulation, 48 rogue Entra devices were registered across victim directories. A registered device gives the attacker a token-generation path that survives session revocation and stays resident until manually deleted.
- Hidden inbox rules are a hallmark of this campaign and a key forensic signal. Rule names observed include ".", "sss", "ss", "iT", ".,.", "........", "s", and "d". Rules filtered or deleted mail containing keywords related to payroll, deposit, and bonus, and routed messages to obscure folders like RSS Feeds and Conversation History. One compromised mailbox had all incoming mail marked read and deleted, then was weaponized to send outbound spam to hundreds of external recipients until Microsoft Entra ID Protection flagged the account as high risk.
- The first observed activity originated from Romanian 🇷🇴 IP 193.26.115[.]221, which VirusTotal associates with AsyncRAT. Token sources span AitM phishing pages, device-code phishing, and social engineering during legitimate login flows. GreyNoise lists 29 IPs matching the hosting provider, with 10 flagged malicious and 5 suspicious. The infrastructure has law enforcement history: StarkRDP and rdp[.]sh domains were seized during Operation Talent in January 2025 alongside Nulled, Cracked, and Sellix.
For responders investigating suspected token replay: audit Entra ID sign-in logs for successful authentications originating from the 193.26.115[.]0/24 range, check the Entra device list for registrations correlating with first-access timestamps, enumerate MFA methods for all accounts and flag changes made within hours of any suspicious sign-in, and pull inbox rules across affected mailboxes hunting for single-character or punctuation-only rule names. Remediation steps include revoking active sessions, resetting credentials, removing rogue devices and MFA registrations, and implementing Conditional Access Policies that enforce MFA unconditionally across all users, all cloud apps, and all client app types to close the device-code workflow abuse path.

item.title: Borrowed Reputation: Domain Shadowing and Gambling SEO
item.description:
Domain shadowing puts illegal gambling pages under .gov and .edu domains in Bangladesh 🇧🇩, India 🇮🇳, and Mexico 🇲🇽, hijacking institutional DNS reputation for SEO without touching the primary website.
- Two separate operations, different DNS techniques. Hidden Hawk added individual CNAME records beneath school and government domains, pointing institutional hostnames to Cloudflare Pages subdomains. The pages[.]dev naming convention mirrored the victim hostname with dots replaced by hyphens, making the relationship reconstructable in passive DNS. A second, unattributed actor targeting maharashtra[.]gov[.]in and online.esic[.]gov[.]in went further: delegating entire subzones (gam, games, search, live, dpboss) to ClouDNS nameservers and using a wildcard under gam.maharashtra[.]gov[.]in, letting the actor generate arbitrary hostnames without touching the government DNS environment again.
- The SEO abuse is the point. Neither operation needed to compromise the victim's primary website. By sitting under .edu.bd and .gov.in namespaces, the doorway pages inherited institutional domain authority and ranked in search results for Indonesian 🇮🇩 gambling brands, rummy, betting, lottery, and satta matka terms. Hidden Hawk operated this as a service, describing backlink optimization and Google AMP landing pages to undercover researchers on Telegram, with pricing quoted in USD and Indonesian 🇮🇩 rupiah alongside Indonesian 🇮🇩 bank details.
- Hidden Hawk's footprint spans more than 850 observed hostnames across eight institutional domains. Actor-operated link-shortening infrastructure (mikale[.]me, hinkale[.]me) and image hosting (imgmahasuhu[.]io, imghaxor[.]io, imgstore[.]io) tied landing pages together. Maharashtra/ESIC content moved through DigitalOcean, then Amazon CloudFront (d9d9t8dndf89z.cloudfront[.]net) and BunnyCDN (search-maharashtra-gov-in.b-cdn[.]net, games-maharashtra-gov-in.b-cdn[.]net, maharashtra-gov-in.b-cdn[.]net). The earlier A record 168.144.156[.]92 has since gone inactive.
- Detection lives in the DNS zone, not the web server. Organizations focused on application logs or uptime monitoring of their primary site would miss this entirely. The victim institutions' main websites stayed up and functional throughout. Evidence to hunt: unexpected NS delegation records in the parent zone, CNAME records pointing to pages[.]dev, netlify[.]app, workers[.]dev, or CDN services with no documented owner, wildcard records, and certificate-transparency entries for hostnames that do not appear in any change record or service inventory.
Practitioners responding to or hunting this class of activity should pull a full export of the authoritative zone and diff it against the approved architecture, not just review forward-lookup results. New NS delegations are the highest-severity finding: once a subzone is delegated out, the parent org loses visibility into every hostname created beneath it. Treat any unrecognized DNS change as a potential credential compromise, rotate DNS-management credentials, enforce MFA on registrar and DNS-provider accounts, and review provider-side access logs for the change event itself. IOCs for both operations are in the Infoblox Threat Intel report.

item.title: PHP2Shell: Suspected North Korean campaign targets 216 vulnerable PHP hosts
item.description:
Suspected North Korean 🇰🇵 operators have identified 216 unpatched PHP hosts vulnerable to two critical RCE flaws, coordinating quietly through I2P while using a local AI model to rank public exploits before striking.
Key details:
- CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both CVSS 9.2, affect all PHP versions handling web requests, with roots in code dating to PHP 5.4. Apache mod_php with prefork is confirmed worst-case for 109618 with full unauthenticated RCE. PHP-FPM via the upload-progress path validates 109619. Critically, disabling session upload progress only mitigates 109619, not 109618: the two bugs need separate stopgaps and should not be treated as one. Working code execution on x86-64 with ASLR enabled has been confirmed against PHP 8.4.10 through 8.4.26. ARM64 achieves memory leaks only so far. Short of RCE, attackers have already demonstrated worker crashes, arbitrary file reads through OPcache, and roughly 67 KB of process memory disclosure. Fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. PHP 5.4 through 7.3 has no fix at all.
- Cyfirma has monitored a private I2P channel since October 22 where two handles active since March 2026 are coordinating the campaign. On October 24 they reported 216 unpatched or partially mitigated hosts and named 21 scan nodes. Scanning is deliberately slow and low-volume, with nodes rotated and any node that triggers rate limiting permanently retired. Rate-based detections will likely stay silent by design. The group has not announced a launch window, but Cyfirma assigns the campaign an imminence score of 78 out of 100.

Priority targets include government and banking, followed by logistics, ports, aviation, manufacturing, and online trading platforms. Technical details leaked October 20, ahead of coordinated disclosure on October 21, and exploitation in the wild dates back to at least October 17. Exploit reliability requires landing a follow-up request on the same worker and shaping heap data, so failed attempts manifest as worker crashes or normal responses, not obvious errors.

Application logs will often be silent because the bug fires before application code runs. The Cyfirma report includes Sigma, Splunk, and YARA detection content, plus defanged lists of 21 scan nodes, 17 source addresses from October 23, and 15 staging addresses. item.title: The Pwn Request Reckoning: What Still Works Against GitHub Actions
item.description:
GitHub Actions' 2026 security overhaul closes the trivial Pwn request path but shifts risk to opt-ins, legacy SHA pins, script injection, and artifact chains that platform controls cannot reach.
Key findings:
- GitHub's phased 2026 rollout delivered four concrete wins: actions/checkout v7 blocks fork code checkout by default for pull_request_target and workflow_run triggers (June 18), read-only cache tokens stop cache poisoning at the platform level (June 26), backports pushed those checkout protections to v2.8.0, v3.7.0, v4.4.0, v5.1.0, and v6.1.0 (July 20), and a default event policy blocking pull_request_target in public repos without an explicit event policy begins enforcement December 2. Critically, private and internal repositories are untouched by the December 2 policy, and workflow_run is not covered.
- SHA pinning, long recommended as supply chain hardening, is now a liability when refs predate the July 20 backport. A workflow pinned to actions/checkout@v4.3.0 or its equivalent commit SHA runs legacy code with no safety checks, while the mutable [@]v4 tag resolves to a protected release. Any SHA ref that predates v2.8.0, v3.7.0, v4.4.0, v5.1.0, or v6.1.0 is unprotected regardless of the tag format used.
- Script injection requires no checkout at all and is untouched by every 2026 change. A pull_request_target workflow that writes ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} directly into a run step hands an attacker shell execution and secrets access with a crafted PR title. The fix is passing untrusted values through environment variables so the shell treats them as data, never as commands. Separately, artifact poisoning chains (an unprivileged pull_request workflow uploads attacker-controlled outputs, a privileged workflow_run downloads and executes them) are also unaffected because artifact access is independent of cache token controls.
- issue_comment and repository_dispatch remain fully exploitable even with checkout v7. GitHub's own changelog notes that checkout protections only cover pull_request_target and workflow_run. Bot-command workflows (/deploy, /test, /cherry-pick) triggered by issue_comment run with secrets and no platform gate. For these, defenders must verify the commenter's actual repository permission via getCollaboratorPermissionLevel (write or above), pin the exact head SHA at the moment the comment fired since refs/pull/N/merge is mutable, and treat all payload fields as untrusted input validated through an anchored allowlist regex passed to the shell via environment variables.
- The "Require approval for all external contributors" Actions setting is widely misunderstood: it gates pull_request workflows (which run the fork's own YAML) but not pull_request_target (which runs the base repo's YAML and is considered trusted). The more dangerous trigger bypasses the human approval gate entirely. Gate privileged pull_request_target jobs behind an environment with required reviewers or restrict actors with Workflow Execution Protections rules.
Practitioner takeaway: Before December 2, run the audit grep the report provides against your .github/workflows/ directory. It flags pull_request_target, workflow_run, issue_comment, repository_dispatch, allow-unsafe-pr-checkout, self-hosted runners, download-artifact calls, direct git clone and gh pr checkout invocations, refs/pull references, outdated checkout versions, and ${{ github.event. }} or ${{ github.head_ref }} interpolations in run steps. Resolve every SHA pin with the companion script in the report to confirm it meets the minimum patched release. For each workflow on your allowlist for the December 2 event policy, re-audit it on every change: those files are precisely the ones handling untrusted input with elevated privileges.

item.title: KillerStrike: Inside an Open-Source Windows RAT
item.description:
KillerStrike, an open-source C/Python Windows RAT shared via Telegram, bundles remote command execution, browser credential theft, file transfers, and A/V capture into a single agent that scored zero detections across ten engines in a scan dated October 22, 2026.
- KillerStrike surfaced in the Telegram group "Exclusive Hacking Tools" (1,544 members at observation) with a direct link to its public GitLab repository under FSEC-VAUL / KillerStrike. The project is self-described as an alpha release, meaning behavior may vary across builds. The agent is a 64-bit PE (~500 KB) written in C; the server runs Flask in Python. Because the source is public, defenders should treat any build, not just the examined agent.exe, as the threat surface.
- Persistence arrives via a Windows service named OptiDiagSvc, presented as "Optimized Diagnostics Service," with the executable dropped under C:\Program Files\Optimized Diagnostics\. That is the default config; both the name and path are operator-configurable. Service creation requires admin rights, which the agent does not self-elevate to obtain (T1543.003).
- Before its first beacon, the agent evaluates uptime, resources, and desktop activity, then watches roughly 15 seconds for keyboard and mouse input while measuring sleep-delay accuracy (T1497). If the score crosses a threshold, the agent holds in a waiting loop. This pre-beacon gate means an endpoint that sees no C2 traffic is not necessarily clean.
- PowerShell execution follows two paths (T1059.001): the agent first hosts a CLR runtime inside its own process, writing a helper DLL named OptDiagCore.dll to the installation or temp directory before invoking it. That path also attempts to modify AMSI and ETW functions in process memory (T1685). If CLR hosting fails, a PowerShell child process launches with an encoded command or a temp .ps1 file. Scripts run in-process leave no powershell.exe child, so a hunt scoped to child-process telemetry alone will miss the primary path.
- Browser collection (T1555.003) prioritizes Login Data before history, bookmarks, and cookies, working against a time budget so credentials are not crowded out by large history databases. The agent handles legacy DPAPI and v10/v11 encrypted records, with a code path for App-Bound v20 data; in the observed test, a v20 entry was identified but remained undecrypted. That single test result does not mean all credentials on a real host would be protected. C2 tasking uses HTTP/HTTPS to /api/agents/register and /api/agents/result at a default 5-second callback interval with +/-25% jitter (T1071.001); HTTPS paths ignore certificate authority and hostname-mismatch errors.
Hunt the default artifacts before reaching for the service name: look for DLL creation and loading of OptDiagCore.dll in installation and temp directories, unfamiliar processes opening Login Data and Local State files with subsequent outbound HTTP, and HTTP requests to the paths /api/agents/register and /api/agents/result. On a confirmed host, collect the service configuration, the agent executable, and relevant logs before remediation, then treat all browser-stored credentials as potentially exposed regardless of the observed App-Bound result.

item.title: uCreator Android Spyware Can Steal Telegram 2FA Passwords and Clone WeChat Accounts
item.description:
Android spyware kit uCreator, linked to Baohuo backdoor reported in October 2025, hooks inside trojanized Telegram and WeChat apps to steal 2FA passwords and clone accounts. Active since at least mid-2024, with developers still committing code in October 2026.
Key findings:
- uCreator's Telegram module matches Doctor Web's Baohuo backdoor exactly: same code namespace com.ucreator.tgjar, same C2, same command names. Baohuo was found in tampered Telegram X copies spreading via in-app ads pointing to fake app store pages, with Portuguese 🇵🇹 and Indonesian 🇮🇩 banners but India 🇮🇳 topping infected-device counts at 22.8%. Copies also appeared on APKPure, ApkSum, and AndroidP, one listed under the real developer's name but with a different digital signature. Doctor Web estimated over 58,000 infected devices as of October 2025.
- The hooking engine runs inside the trojanized app with the signed-in app's own identity and permissions. For Telegram, it intercepts the two-step verification (2FA) password before the app hashes it, captures it in plaintext, and can then reset sessions, swap the linked phone number, or delete the account. The attacker's session is hidden from the device list the tampered app shows the user. The backdoor also exfiltrates the account's phone number, name, and password to C2 every three minutes. For WeChat, the kit runs the unmodified app inside its own virtualization container, zips the account's login identity and data, uploads it, and uses a bundled script to clone the account.
- A leaked GitLab back end, left exposed without IP restrictions, reveals a cloud console rented to merchants and resellers. Each customer's commands carry their own ID, letting them direct activity against victims they select. A scheduler enforces time windows, random daily limits, and per-account budgets to mimic human behavior and evade platform risk checks. The code names this "account cultivation." About three dozen developers working on China 🇨🇳 time appear in the commit history, with changes still landing in October 2026. Attribution points to three companies in Hunan province.
- The newest sample is dated July 29, 2026. The hooking engine fails on Android 17 because a required internal function changed, but Frida can still perform the same hook on that version, so Android 17 is not a hard block. Samples built for Android 16 exist. The kit targets roughly 20 apps including WeCom, QQ, WhatsApp, LINE, Zalo, KakaoTalk, Viber, GCash, and MoMo, though published module code covers only Telegram and WeChat so far.
- Two reliable host-based indicators: the file TgJarPine.dex in the assets directory of tampered Telegram copies, and the original app copy LSPatch leaves at cache/lspatch/origin/*.apk. One C2-adjacent IP still resolved on October 23, 2026: version-upload domain hw[.]android.videoflow[.]cn pointing to 121.37.194[.]194. Other notable infrastructure includes relay IP 43.225.141[.]209 used by the Telegram part and hook download URL kfpt.oss-cn-hangzhou.aliyuncs[.]com/android/app/YingGai/. Eight sample hashes and the full IOC set are in the report.
Takeaway for responders: on any Android device under investigation, check the assets folder of installed Telegram or WeChat packages for TgJarPine.dex and look for cache/lspatch/origin/*.apk, which indicates LSPatch was used to trojanize the app. Cross-reference installed package names against the report's hashes, especially org.thunderdog.challegram and org.telegram.messenger[.]web, since the tampered copies reuse legitimate package names. If you are investigating a compromised Telegram account, the hiding of attacker sessions means the victim's own device list inside a tampered app cannot be trusted: advise the victim to check session lists from a known-clean, unmodified Telegram client. Doctor Web has also published its own Baohuo indicators separately.

item.title: Gheist Uses Stolen GitHub Tokens to Steal Private Repository Secrets via Actions Logs
item.description:
Automated campaign Gheist has planted secret-stealing GitHub Actions workflows in 850+ compromised accounts since September 15, successfully exfiltrating secrets from private repos and GitHub Enterprise environments where GitHub's approval safeguard does not apply.
Key findings:
- Gheist operates by using stolen tokens (sourced from infostealer logs and prior supply-chain compromises, including the March Trivy scanner breach) to push a single workflow file, .github/workflows/sync-check.yml, to a new branch named ci-sync- followed by six random characters, with the commit message "ci: sync config". The workflow calls toJSON(secrets) and pipes output through base32 encoding, which bypasses GitHub's secret-masking because the encoded value no longer matches the stored secret. Logs are downloaded via GitHub's API and the run deleted seconds later. No attacker-controlled server receives the traffic: exfiltration moves entirely through GitHub's own infrastructure, eliminating a network-based detection path.
- GitHub's workflow approval hold, active since July 28, stopped every public-repository Gheist run Wiz examined, but GitHub's own documentation confirms it applies only to public repositories on github[.]com. Private repositories and GitHub Enterprise Server have no equivalent control, and those are exactly where Wiz confirmed successful runs. Audit logs in private environments show ci-sync- branch runs completing and then being deleted by the user agent "gheist" within a minute.
- One variant pushes a second job targeting self-hosted runners, scanning for 31 credential types: private keys, process environments, AWS instance role credentials, runner credential files (.gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg, .gdmp_sweep), and Kubernetes service account tokens. Wiz describes this job as buggy with no confirmed successful run, but its presence signals the campaign is actively expanding scope. On October 19 and 20, three victim accounts also re-pushed Gheist commits with a loader injected into vite.config.js, a file pattern researchers associate with North Korean 🇰🇵 PolinRider malware.
- If your workflows use OIDC to authenticate to a cloud provider, ci-sync- branch names appear in the token subject, giving you a detection path even without GitHub log collection. Check AWS CloudTrail for role assumptions or STS token exchanges whose subject field contains ci-sync-. Wiz observed cloud credentials from compromised organizations being used to enumerate AWS Secrets Manager hours after the branch was planted, though the report does not attribute that access definitively to Gheist's workflow output.
- The report publishes four git blob SHAs for known workflow variants (f3da2b8b357dcda02fd455d314be2a95007516a6, d09535857a741bbb976bdc084a9a021713133291, 1dc5af9cce950aad1eb1546ecce8565b117540c4, c665b778b2d822453293003e7ca0bbb2cb08e39d), the user agent string "gheist", the branch regex ^ci-sync-[0-9a-z]{6}$, and the self-hosted runner artifact strings (.gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg, .gdmp_sweep, gdmp-pivot). Deleting the branch or the run does not undo secret exposure; every secret the repository could reach during the run must be rotated and the token that pushed the branch revoked.
Practitioner takeaway: Start in your GitHub audit log. Filter for workflow runs on branches matching ci-sync-* that were deleted within 60 seconds of completion, and separately for any event carrying the user agent "gheist". Cross-reference in CloudTrail or your cloud provider's equivalent: OIDC subject strings containing ci-sync- confirm the Actions job ran and assumed a cloud role. On self-hosted runners, hunt for .gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg, and .gdmp_sweep on disk, and grep job logs for gdmp-pivot. If you find a ci-sync- branch, rotate all secrets the repository could read, revoke the committing token immediately, and check that token owner's device for infostealer infection. IOCs and workflow blob SHAs are in Wiz's report.

item.content:encoded:
Automated campaign Gheist has planted secret-stealing GitHub Actions workflows in 850+ compromised accounts since September 15, successfully exfiltrating secrets from private repos and GitHub Enterprise environments where GitHub's approval safeguard does not apply.

Key findings:

- Gheist operates by using stolen tokens (sourced from infostealer logs and prior supply-chain compromises, including the March Trivy scanner breach) to push a single workflow file, .github/workflows/sync-check.yml, to a new branch named ci-sync- followed by six random characters, with the commit message "ci: sync config". The workflow calls toJSON(secrets) and pipes output through base32 encoding, which bypasses GitHub's secret-masking because the encoded value no longer matches the stored secret. Logs are downloaded via GitHub's API and the run deleted seconds later. No attacker-controlled server receives the traffic: exfiltration moves entirely through GitHub's own infrastructure, eliminating a network-based detection path.

- GitHub's workflow approval hold, active since July 28, stopped every public-repository Gheist run Wiz examined, but GitHub's own documentation confirms it applies only to public repositories on github[.]com. Private repositories and GitHub Enterprise Server have no equivalent control, and those are exactly where Wiz confirmed successful runs. Audit logs in private environments show ci-sync- branch runs completing and then being deleted by the user agent "gheist" within a minute.

- One variant pushes a second job targeting self-hosted runners, scanning for 31 credential types: private keys, process environments, AWS instance role credentials, runner credential files (.gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg, .gdmp_sweep), and Kubernetes service account tokens. Wiz describes this job as buggy with no confirmed successful run, but its presence signals the campaign is actively expanding scope. On October 19 and 20, three victim accounts also re-pushed Gheist commits with a loader injected into vite.config.js, a file pattern researchers associate with North Korean 🇰🇵 PolinRider malware.

- If your workflows use OIDC to authenticate to a cloud provider, ci-sync- branch names appear in the token subject, giving you a detection path even without GitHub log collection. Check AWS CloudTrail for role assumptions or STS token exchanges whose subject field contains ci-sync-. Wiz observed cloud credentials from compromised organizations being used to enumerate AWS Secrets Manager hours after the branch was planted, though the report does not attribute that access definitively to Gheist's workflow output.

- The report publishes four git blob SHAs for known workflow variants (f3da2b8b357dcda02fd455d314be2a95007516a6, d09535857a741bbb976bdc084a9a021713133291, 1dc5af9cce950aad1eb1546ecce8565b117540c4, c665b778b2d822453293003e7ca0bbb2cb08e39d), the user agent string "gheist", the branch regex ^ci-sync-[0-9a-z]{6}$, and the self-hosted runner artifact strings (.gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg, .gdmp_sweep, gdmp-pivot). Deleting the branch or the run does not undo secret exposure; every secret the repository could reach during the run must be rotated and the token that pushed the branch revoked.

Practitioner takeaway: Start in your GitHub audit log. Filter for workflow runs on branches matching ci-sync-* that were deleted within 60 seconds of completion, and separately for any event carrying the user agent "gheist". Cross-reference in CloudTrail or your cloud provider's equivalent: OIDC subject strings containing ci-sync- confirm the Actions job ran and assumed a cloud role. On self-hosted runners, hunt for .gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg, and .gdmp_sweep on disk, and grep job logs for gdmp-pivot. If you find a ci-sync- branch, rotate all secrets the repository could read, revoke the committing token immediately, and check that token owner's device for infostealer infection. IOCs and workflow blob SHAs are in Wiz's report.

item.title: Beyond testmetest: Native Addon Camouflage and 42 Armed GitHub Repositories Reveal a Hidden npm Publisher
item.description:
The testmetest npm campaign armed 42 real GitHub repositories across 11 legitimate owners, deployed a native addon camouflage to bypass static analysis, and linked its infrastructure to active CVE-2026-41940 exploitation of internet-facing cPanel systems.
Key findings:
- The campaign spread through the npm ecosystem via 25 package names and 82 known version records, using a binding.gyp command expansion to execute during installation without declaring a conventional install script. The full-worm bundle (seen in event-bus-lite-testmetest@0.0.2 and others) stole GitHub and npm credentials, poisoned repository CI configs, and self-propagated through package registries. A separate ci.js publisher used GitHub OIDC token exchange with hxxps[:]//registry.npmjs[.]org to mint npm publishing tokens from compromised Actions contexts, explaining how clean-looking default branches could produce malicious registry releases.
- Three packages, [@]iobandamwer/cache-helper, [@]iobandamwer/native-helper and path-stream-utils-testmetest, dropped a compiled native addon (addon.node, addon_win.node) and a dotfile .napi_cache beside it. The addon XORs .napi_cache with 0x96 at runtime to recover a JavaScript payload, writes it to /tmp/. on Linux or %TEMP%\.nc .js on Windows (hidden attribute set), and launches it detached via node with no console window. No cleanup code was found, so the dropped file persists. The Windows build gates execution against process memory over 1.5 GB, processor count, IsDebuggerPresent, and running processes including wireshark, procmon, procexp, x64dbg, ollydbg, fiddler and httpdebug.
- GitHub code search missed the armed repositories entirely because the polymorphic wrapper blobs ranged from 12.9 to 13.7 MB, exceeding both the search index and the contents API size limits. All 42 repositories were only found by enumerating Git trees and fetching blobs directly. All 10 distinct wrapper builds (ROT keys 1 through 22) decode to the same 2 MB payload with SHA-256 9d83919bfdb0e14018f1a6f2b8b6586de59b60dfdcfbdb5ae1a1556c23cc4793. Execution was triggered by hooking .claude/settings.json, .gemini/settings.json, .cursor/mcp.json, .cursor/rules/setup.mdc and .vscode/tasks.json, turning any developer opening a workspace into a detonation event.
- The attacker-controlled CementBeetleSteeple/stable-scripts-9965 repository was an active encrypted data sink holding 27 data/snap-*.json files (384,825 bytes total) committed with the message "chore: sync" between October 22 and October 24. Fake CodeQL workflows named scan-output dumped base64-encoded environment variables including real npm tokens to one-day artifacts. September 28 arming batches copied legitimate author dates and commit messages and appended skip-checks:true, forging a historical-looking timeline across hijacked accounts including leamasuero (a real Argentine 🇦🇷 developer active since 2013) and the Crayon-Biz-LLP organization.
- Shellpanel workflows in the same hijacked owner cluster targeted CVE-2026-41940, an authentication bypass in cPanel & WHM and WP Squared added to the CISA KEV catalog in April 2026. The workflow under hakimrasdi/2310-ICT602 downloaded a binary from hxxp[:]//43.228.157[.]68:80/api/dl/ to /tmp/.svc and ran it with 1,000 workers, a count of 9,999,999,999 and --exploit CVE-2026-41940 against cPanel ports 80, 443, 2082, 2083, 2086, 2087, 2095, 2096, 2077 and 2078.
Responder action: Do not rely on GitHub code search or the contents API to clear a repository, enumerate Git trees and blobs directly. Hunt repositories for .github/init.js, all five AI and IDE hook files, skip-checks:true commit trailers, chore/ci- and deps/upd- branches, and the scan-output artifact. On hosts, look for .napi_cache next to any installed addon.node, check /tmp/ for hidden dot-files and %TEMP%\.nc .js, and check persistence under net-health-checker and pkg-runtime LaunchAgents and systemd user services before revoking stolen tokens (the worm contains a token-revocation wiper). Block 43.228.157[.]68:80 and hxxps[:]//aiarmor[.]website/v1/api. Full IOC table and SHA-256 hashes are in the JFrog report.
